summary: Verdict: do NOT try to follow all ~8,000 followers of "Shadows of Rumelia". There are three reasons. (1) Instagram's own Help Center caps following at 7,500 accounts, so "following 8,000" can only work if you also unfollow. That is the follow/unfollow pattern that Meta's Spam policy (posting or engaging "manually or automatically, at very high frequencies") and audit tools like HypeAuditor flag. (2) Instagram publishes no daily or hourly follow limits. Third-party 2025-2026 estimates for brand-new accounts cluster around 20-60 follows per day and about 10 per hour. At those rates 8,000 follows takes roughly 5 to 13 months and about 50+ hours of tapping. (3) The payoff is poor and unproven. I found no independent follow-back data for Instagram. The vendor and anecdotal numbers I did find run from 3% (an X/Twitter dataset, June 2026) to 12% for manual follows (an old vendor blog). That means roughly 240-960 low-intent "reciprocity" followers who mostly will not like your posts. Mosseri said in May 2026 that like rates matter most for distribution to followers and send rates matter most for non-followers. He also said removing inactive or bot followers "is not going to affect your reach", and that Reels get a first test audience whether or not people follow you. So a padded follower count does not buy reach and can dilute it. The biggest risk is losing recommendation eligibility. Instagram's Help Center says accounts that "repeatedly engaged in misleading practices to build followings" and content boosted by "coordinated comment networks" are not recommended, and a zero-follower account grows almost entirely through recommendations. A better way to reach the competitor's audience: write substantive comments on the competitor's and larger adjacent accounts' posts, reply to their most active commenters, follow 10-25 of those active commenters a day after you have interacted with them, propose Collab posts with the competitor or with Balkan/muhacir associations, and use comment-to-DM only through Meta-approved API tools. Avoid engagement pods, bought followers, follow-for-follow groups and "follow + tag to win" giveaways. In Turkey, any giveaway (çekiliş) needs Milli Piyango İdaresi permission, and the Finance Minister said in January 2025 that running one without permission carries 3-6 years in prison. If the user still wants to follow people, a capped, manual, warm-target protocol is given in the last finding.

findings.claim: Following all ~8,000 followers of a competitor is impossible as a 'follow and keep' plan because Instagram hard-caps following at 7,500. It only works as a follow-then-unfollow cycle, which is the behavior Meta's Spam policy and third-party audit tools target.
findings.detail: Instagram Help Center (help article 408167069251249, read via the facebook.com/help/instagram mirror on 2026-11-03) says: "To help reduce spam, Instagram doesn't allow anyone to follow more than 7,500 people" and "Anyone who tries to follow more than 7,500 people will see an error message, regardless of how many followers they have." Meta's Community Standards on Spam (latest dated change-log entry Jun 26, 2024) prohibit "Posting, sharing, engaging with content or creating accounts..." "manually or automatically, at very high frequencies". They add that Meta "may place restrictions on accounts that are acting at lower frequencies when other indicators of Spam" are present. So doing it by hand is no defense. Instagram's old Community Guidelines URL (help.instagram.com/477434105621119) now 301-redirects to Meta's Community Standards (observed 2026-11-03). HypeAuditor's help article (dated Jul 13, 2026) calls follow/unfollow "a direct violation of Instagram's Terms and Conditions and Community Guidelines" and says "Spikes on the Followings Growth graph are a clear indicator". Brand-audit tools therefore mark such accounts publicly as using artificial growth.
findings.recommendation: Drop the 'follow all 8,000' plan. Never let the following count approach the cap. Do not run follow/unfollow cycles. Replace it with small daily batches of warm, targeted follows (see P15) and engagement-led tactics (P10-P12).
sources: https://transparency.meta.com/policies/community-standards/spam/ (Meta Spam policy; last dated change Jun 26, 2024)
findings.verify_note: I re-read every cited source on 2026-11-04. The Instagram Help Center mirror (facebook.com/help/instagram/408167069251249) says, word for word: "To help reduce spam, Instagram doesn't allow anyone to follow more than 7,500 people". It adds that anyone who tries to go past that limit "will see an error message, regardless of how many followers they have". It also notes that accounts already following more than 7,500 before the rule are not affected. Meta's Spam policy matches the quotes: "Posting, sharing, engaging with content or creating accounts... either manually or automatically, at very high frequencies" and "We may place restrictions on accounts that are acting at lower frequencies". The newest dated change-log entry is still Jun 26, 2024. I ran curl -I on help.instagram.com/477434105621119: it returns HTTP 301 to transparency.meta.com/policies/community-standards/. The HypeAuditor article quotes are verbatim. The page shows "Jul 13, 2026, Written by Iren" without saying whether that is the publication or update date. One caveat: the claim that the plan "only works as follow-then-unfollow" is the researcher's reasoning from the cap, not an Instagram statement. The reasoning is sound.

findings.claim: Instagram does not publish daily or hourly follow limits. Limits are dynamic and stricter for new accounts. Third-party 2025-2026 estimates put a cautious new account at about 20-60 follows per day and about 10 (at most 10-20) per hour, with temporary action blocks when exceeded.
findings.detail: SocialRails (published Jan 15, 2025, updated Jul 21, 2026): "Instagram does not publish a daily or hourly follow limit, and it never has." Its community estimates: new accounts (under a few months old) about 20-60 per day, established accounts about 150-200 per day, pacing about 10-20 per hour. Unfollr, a vendor (Jun 6, 2026): accounts 0-3 months old 7-13 per hour and 50-100 per day, and it advises halving all limits for accounts under 6 months. It says Instagram 'keeps them deliberately vague'. Its typical block ladder (not official): 30 min to a few hours, then 24 h, then 48 h to 1 week, then weeks or permanent. Metricool (Jan 21, 2026): about 150 per day general and 'around 10 per hour' pacing, with no separate new-account follow figure. Tagembed (2026) claims '50 follows in 5 minutes' gets flagged even under daily caps but gives no source. All of these numbers are folk estimates from testing. None is confirmed by Meta.
findings.recommendation: For a brand-new account (launch 2026-11-04), treat 20-30 follows per day as the ceiling for the first month and keep it to 10 or fewer per hour, spread over 3-4 sessions. If you see 'We limit how often you can do certain things' / 'Try again later', stop all following for 48-72 hours.
findings.verify_note: Every number matches its source. SocialRails (published Jan 15, 2025, updated Jul 21, 2026) says "Instagram does not publish a daily or hourly follow limit, and it never has". It gives about 20-60 follows a day for new accounts, about 150-200 for established ones, and 10-20 an hour as a pacing habit, not an enforced cap. Unfollr (Jun 6, 2026) gives 7-13 an hour and 50-100 a day for accounts 0-3 months old, advises halving every limit for accounts under 6 months, and describes the same block ladder. It adds that 48-hour to week-long blocks may require identity confirmation. Metricool (Jan 21, 2026) gives about 150 a day and about 10 an hour, with no separate new-account follow figure. Tagembed is dated Jul 2, 2026. It says "following 50 accounts in 5 minutes is flagged even if you haven't hit your daily cap" and cites no source. All of these are community estimates, not Meta figures.

findings.claim: Automation and third-party growth apps are explicitly off-limits. Meta bans exchanging follows for engagement, Instagram's Terms ban automated access without permission, and Instagram says it removes automated likes, comments and follows created by third-party apps.
findings.detail: Meta Spam policy bans "Attempting to or successfully selling, buying, or exchanging for engagement, such as likes, shares, views, follows" (it also covers clicks and hashtags). Instagram Terms of Use section 4.2 (read via the facebook.com mirror, 2026-11-03; no effective date shown) bans accessing or collecting information "in an automated way without our express permission". Instagram's Help Center page on follower/like changes says "non-Instagram apps create automated likes, comments and follows" and that this activity "is removed from Instagram". Background: Instagram's Nov 2018 announcement 'Reducing Inauthentic Activity' said it uses machine learning to find accounts using such apps, removes the inauthentic follows, and warns that accounts that continue 'may see their Instagram experience impacted'. I found no official Meta document describing a new 2026 automation crackdown. Several 2026 vendor blogs claim enforcement got stricter after late 2025, but they cite no Meta source.
findings.recommendation: Use no auto-follow, auto-like or 'mass unfollow' apps, browser extensions or Telegram bots, and never give any tool the account password. If you use any automation, it must be a Meta API-based tool that connects through official Facebook/Instagram login (see P12).
findings.verify_note: Instagram Terms of Use, section 4.2: "creating accounts or accessing or collecting information in an automated way without our express permission". The clause applies even when you are logged in. The page shows no effective date, only "(c) 2026 Meta". Help Center 572730176521116: "Sometimes, non-Instagram apps create automated likes, comments and follows to make an account appear more popular than it is" and "When these accounts are discovered, their activity is removed from Instagram." The Instagram blog post 'Reducing Inauthentic Activity' is dated Nov 19, 2018, and the researcher's paraphrases of it are accurate. The Spam policy's ban on exchanging engagement lists likes, shares, views, follows, clicks and use of specific hashtags. I also found no Meta document announcing a new automation crackdown in 2026, though my web search was unavailable (see missed points).

findings.claim: For a new page, the real risk is not a 24-hour action block but losing recommendation eligibility, because a zero-follower account grows almost entirely through recommendations to non-followers.
findings.detail: Instagram Help Center (Recommendations, help article 313829416281232, accessed 2026-11-03) lists accounts that are not eligible to be recommended. These include accounts that "Repeatedly engaged in misleading practices to build followings, such as purchasing 'likes'" and accounts that "Recently violated Instagram's Community Guidelines". Content that is not eligible includes engagement from "coordinated comment networks intended to artificially drive engagement and distribution" and "Unoriginal content that is largely repurposed from another source" (relevant to history pages that repost archival images without adding anything). Instagram's Creators blog (Aug 30, 2022, updated Apr 25, 2023) warns that "your entire account may become ineligible for recommendation". Mosseri's 'Instagram Ranking Explained' (May 31, 2023): in Explore, "Most of the content you'll see... is from people you don't follow"; in Reels, "the majority of what you see is from accounts you don't follow". Professional accounts can check eligibility under Settings > Account > Account Status.
findings.recommendation: Treat recommendation eligibility as the page's most valuable asset. Switch to a Creator/Professional account on day 1, check Account Status weekly, and avoid anything that looks like misleading follower-building or pods. Add your own research, maps or sources to archival images instead of reposting them bare.
findings.verify_note: The quotes from the recommendations guidelines (facebook.com/help/instagram/313829416281232) are verbatim: "Repeatedly engaged in misleading practices to build followings, such as purchasing 'likes'", "Recently violated Instagram's Community Guidelines", "coordinated comment networks intended to artificially drive engagement and distribution", and "Unoriginal content that is largely repurposed from another source with only minor, immaterial edits". The Creators blog is dated Aug 30, 2022, updated Apr 25, 2023, and contains "your entire account may become ineligible for recommendation". 'Instagram Ranking Explained' (May 31, 2023) confirms that most Explore and Reels content comes from accounts you don't follow. Small fix: the Account Status Help page the researcher cites (539126347315373) does not mention recommendation eligibility. The eligibility check is described in the Creators blog (Settings > Account > Account Status, professional accounts). The current Help page gives the path as More > Settings > Account Status. The claim that a zero-follower account grows "almost entirely" through recommendations is inference, but it fits the sources.

findings.claim: There is no credible, independent data on Instagram follow-back rates. The only numbers come from vendors or old anecdotal tests, and they range from about 3% to about 30%. One controlled comparison found bot-driven follow/unfollow underperformed organic growth.
findings.detail: No peer-reviewed or platform data was found (searched 'follow-back rate Instagram study/experiment', 'follow-for-follow reciprocity research'). Anecdotal and vendor figures: (a) Block AI on dev.to (Jun 11, 2026, X/Twitter, not Instagram; the author's company sells follow automation): 9,418 follows across 11 accounts gave a 3.0% follow-back rate (6,127-follow matured cohort), with 5.6% for targets with 1k-10k followers. (b) A vendor post on cnblogs (circa 2018, automation seller): 1,000 manual follows in a fitness niche gave about 12% follow-back, versus about 31% with its automation. These are self-reported. (c) Agorapulse Social Media Lab (Nov 2017 to Apr 2018): follower growth of 101-698% on 4 accounts using follow/unfollow, but no follow-back percentage reported and the period predates current enforcement. (d) Animalz test published on AdEspresso (Jan 24, 2019): a follow/unfollow bot gained 4.1 followers/day versus 9.3/day organic, earned under half the likes, about 4 vs 10 comments/day, and produced no sales. Applying 3-12% to 8,000 follows suggests roughly 240-960 follow-backs (my arithmetic on weak data).
findings.recommendation: Do not plan around follow-backs. If you test following at all, log follows and follow-backs in a sheet for 2 weeks and judge on your own number. Also measure whether those people ever like or comment, not just whether they follow.
findings.verify_note: (a) dev.to: posted Jun 11, 2026 by Harvey Stone, using Block AI's internal data from Jun 1-10, 2026, on X, not Instagram. It reports 9,418 follows from 11 accounts, a 3.0% follow-back rate on the 6,127 follows at least 72 hours old (3.1% raw), and 5.6% for targets with 1k-10k followers. Block AI sells X follow automation (GeniusX/CloneX). (b) cnblogs: a repost dated Sep 6, 2018 with no original date. It claims 12% follow-back for manual follows versus 31% with automation, with no methodology, from an author who promotes automation. (c) Agorapulse: Instagram accounts tested between Nov 28, 2017 and Apr 30, 2018, with growth of 101-698% and no follow-back rate. The page was last modified Dec 23, 2025. (d) AdEspresso/Animalz (Jan 24, 2019): a Boostgram follow/like/unfollow bot gained 4.1 followers a day versus 9.3 organic. Likes were under 100 a day versus over 200 (about half), comments about 4 versus 10 a day, and there were no sales. The 240-960 arithmetic is correct.

findings.claim: Mosseri and Instagram have repeatedly said follower count does not decide reach. Distribution is tested post by post on engagement per viewer, and in May 2026 Mosseri said removing inactive or bot followers will not affect reach. Nuance: Instagram's 2023 explainer still lists follower count as one popularity signal for Reels.
findings.detail: May 2026 'great purge': Mosseri, in an Instagram Stories Q&A reported around May 8, 2026, said "we regularly remove accounts that are either very very long inactive or bots", "it's not going to affect your reach" and "It's not actual real followers that you have lost" (whatson.ae, May 14, 2026). Social Media Today (May 26, 2026) quotes Mosseri: "So of all the people who saw the post, how many of them actually engaged with that post?" and "like rates matter more for your followers, and send rates matter more for those who don't follow you." Social Media Today (Apr 2, 2024) summarizes a Mosseri Threads post: engagement matters more than follower counts, "which can be gamed, cheated". Engadget (Apr 30, 2024): Instagram said eligible Reels are shown to a small audience "regardless of whether they follow the account that posted it or not", and top performers then get wider distribution. January 2025 (Social Media Today): Mosseri named watch time, likes per reach and sends per reach as the top signals. Nuance: 'Instagram Ranking Explained' (May 31, 2023) says Reels consider "popularity signals such as number of followers or level of engagement", so follower count is not zero-weight, but it is one signal among many.
findings.recommendation: Optimize for watch time, sends and likes per viewer, not for follower count. One highly 'sendable' Reel or carousel (for example a map of 1912 Rumeli kazas, or 'which village did your family leave in 93 Harbi/1912?') reaches non-followers regardless of your follower number.
findings.verify_note: The quotes are verified: whatson.ae (May 14, 2026), Social Media Today (May 26, 2026), Engadget (Apr 30, 2024) and Ranking Explained (May 31, 2023), which says follower count is one Reels popularity signal. Corrections: (1) The summary credits Mosseri in May 2026 with the point that Reels get a first test audience whether or not people follow you. That statement comes from Instagram's April 2024 announcement as reported by Engadget. (2) The Social Media Today article of Apr 2, 2024 does not quote Mosseri. "which can be gamed, cheated, etc." is the SMT writer's summary of a Threads post embedded as an image. (3) The January 2025 article is dated Jan 22, 2025. Mosseri's words were "watch time, likes and sends"; 'likes per reach / sends per reach' is his advice on what to check in Insights. (4) Gulf News (last updated May 7, 2026) contains no Mosseri quote. It only reports the cleanup.
findings.corrected_claim: Mosseri (whatson.ae, May 14, 2026) said Instagram "regularly remove[s] accounts that are either very very long inactive or bots" and that "it's not going to affect your reach". He also said (Social Media Today, May 26, 2026) that "like rates matter more for your followers, and send rates matter more for those who don't follow you." Separately, Instagram itself (Engadget, Apr 30, 2024), not Mosseri in May 2026, said Reels are first shown to a small audience "regardless of whether they follow the account". In January 2025 (Social Media Today, Jan 22, 2025) Mosseri named "watch time, likes and sends" as the top three signals.

findings.claim: Follow-back followers gained through reciprocity, not interest, likely dilute the follower like-rate that drives distribution to followers. A large following count also looks spammy to human visitors and brand-audit tools, although no official source says the follower/following ratio is a ranking factor.
findings.detail: Inference: per Mosseri (May 26, 2026), like rate among followers drives connected distribution. Hundreds of reciprocity followers who never engage lower the share of followers who like each post. No official Instagram source was found saying the ratio itself is ranked. Unfollr (Jun 14, 2026) says "Instagram doesn't directly use the ratio in its ranking algorithm" and cites no Instagram documentation for its indirect 'trust score' claims. Perception is real, though: HypeAuditor (Jul 13, 2026) auto-flags spikes in following, and a profile showing, say, '3,000 following / 400 followers' signals 'I follow to get followed' to the history-literate audience you want. Practical side effect: following thousands of random accounts floods your own feed and makes the daily engagement work in P10 harder.
findings.recommendation: Keep following deliberate and modest (for example, under about 1,000 in the first months), made up of relevant history, Balkan, muhacir and academic accounts you actually interact with. A high-quality small audience beats a padded large one.
sources: no source; reasoning (dilution effect is inference)
findings.verify_note: Unfollr (Jun 14, 2026) says "Instagram doesn't directly use the ratio in its ranking algorithm" and "The ratio itself isn't a ranking signal". It cites no source for its 'trust score' claims, exactly as the researcher said. I found no official Instagram source saying the follower/following ratio is a ranking factor. The dilution effect is clearly labelled as inference, and it follows from Mosseri's May 26, 2026 remark that like rate among followers drives distribution to followers. The 'under about 1,000 following' ceiling is the researcher's own heuristic and has no source.

findings.claim: Time cost: at cautious new-account rates, 8,000 manual follows take about 5 to 13 months and roughly 40-55 hours of hands-on time, for a projected 240-960 low-intent follow-backs.
findings.detail: My arithmetic on the P2 estimates: 8,000 ÷ 20/day = 400 days; ÷ 30/day ≈ 267 days (about 9 months); ÷ 50/day = 160 days (about 5.3 months); ÷ 100/day = 80 days (about 11-12 weeks, but 100/day is above the cautious range for an account under 6 months). Any plan beyond 7,500 also needs unfollows, which roughly doubles the actions. Hands-on time: if each follow includes a quick profile check (about 20-25 s), that is about 45-55 hours. Pure tapping at about 5 s is about 11 hours, but rapid-fire tapping is exactly the burst pattern that triggers blocks. Payoff using the P5 range (3-12%): about 240-960 follow-backs, or about 20-90 per month at 25 follows/day.
findings.recommendation: Put those hours into content and community work instead. 45-55 hours equals about 3 months of a 30-minute daily engagement routine (P10) plus several Collab pitches (P11), which reach active, interested people rather than random follower lists.
sources: no source; reasoning (arithmetic based on https://socialrails.com/blog/instagram-follow-limits-explained and https://www.unfollr.com/blog/instagram-follow-unfollow-limits)
findings.verify_note: I rechecked the arithmetic. 8,000 / 20 = 400 days (13.1 months). 8,000 / 30 = 267 days. 8,000 / 50 = 160 days (5.3 months). 8,000 / 100 = 80 days (11.4 weeks). At 20-25 s per follow, 8,000 follows take 44-56 hours; at 5 s, 11 hours. 25 follows a day is about 750 a month, which gives about 22-90 follow-backs a month at 3-12%. The inputs are consistent with the P2 sources: Unfollr's 50-100 a day for 0-3-month accounts, halved for accounts under 6 months, gives 25-50, and SocialRails gives 20-60. The 3% input is X/Twitter data, which weakens the projection.

findings.claim: A competitor's follower list is a poor targeting pool. It contains inactive accounts, bots, passive followers and possibly people who do not read Turkish. The competitor's ACTIVE commenters are the high-value subset.
findings.detail: Not found: I could not verify the 'Shadows of Rumelia' account, its handle, language or follower count (searched '"Shadows of Rumelia" instagram'; Instagram profiles are not indexed without login). The ~8,000 figure is the user's. The English name suggests a possibly mixed international or Balkan audience; this is unverified. The May 2026 cleanup, which Mosseri described as removing 'very very long inactive' accounts and bots, shows that large follower pools normally contain many such accounts. Anyone who commented on a Rumeli/Balkan history post in the last 2-4 weeks has shown they are active and interested in the topic.
findings.recommendation: Before any outreach, open 50 random followers of the competitor and count how many are Turkish-speaking, active (posted or commented recently) and real. Then shift targeting to people who commented on the competitor's and similar pages' last 10-20 posts.
sources: no source; reasoning (account could not be verified)
findings.verify_note: I also could not verify 'Shadows of Rumelia'. My guessed URL instagram.com/shadowsofrumelia returned HTTP 429 to WebFetch. My web search budget was exhausted on my first query, and the rules forbid fetching through third-party Instagram viewers. Handle, language and the roughly 8,000 followers therefore remain unverified; the figure is the user's own. The rest of the claim is reasonable but rests on inference. The May 2026 removal of 'very very long inactive' accounts and bots (whatson.ae, May 14, 2026) supports the idea that large follower lists contain dead accounts. No source quantifies the inactive share of this competitor's audience.

findings.claim: The most effective organic way to reach a competitor's audience is to show up where it is active. Write substantive comments on the competitor's and larger adjacent pages' new posts, reply to the people commenting there, and work keyword or hashtag search results, so curious people click through to your profile.
findings.detail: Reasoning, partly backed by Instagram signals. Mosseri's top signals (Jan 2025: watch time, likes per reach, sends per reach) and May 2026 remarks mean a strong profile converts visitors. A good comment under a popular post is a free billboard seen by that post's audience. Instagram caps hashtags at 5 per post/Reel and Mosseri frames hashtags as a search aid, not a reach booster (reported Dec 19, 2025), so use hashtags and keywords for discoverability only. I found no controlled study quantifying followers gained per comment; this is practitioner logic, and creator blogs attribute 'respond to comments' advice to Mosseri without primary quotes. Avoid copy-paste or emoji comments: Meta's spam policy targets repetitive engagement, and the recommendations guidelines target coordinated comment networks.
findings.recommendation: Daily 30-45 min routine: (1) comment early (within the first hour) on 10-15 posts from the competitor and bigger adjacent accounts (Ottoman/Balkan history, Western Thrace, Bulgarian Turks, muhacir/mübadil associations, Kosovo/Macedonia/Bosnia Turkish communities). Each comment should add a specific fact, date, place or source in 2-3 sentences, never 'great post, check my page'. (2) Reply thoughtfully to 5-10 commenters under those posts. (3) Search Turkish keywords (Rumeli, muhacir, mübadele, 93 Harbi, Balkan Savaşı, Batı Trakya, Deliorman, Kırcaali, Üsküp, Selanik) and engage on the top recent posts. (4) Use at most 5 precise hashtags. (5) Have 9-12 strong posts plus a clear bio and highlights live before driving traffic, so visitors convert.
sources: no source; reasoning (comment-to-follower conversion not quantified anywhere I found)
findings.verify_note: Business Today (Dec 19, 2025) reports that Instagram cut the hashtag maximum "from 30 to just 5" for posts and Reels, and that some users briefly saw a cap of 3 during testing. It says Mosseri "has recently reiterated that hashtags are no longer the primary driver of reach", with caption keywords, on-screen text and visuals weighted more heavily. Metricool (Jan 21, 2026) also says "up to 5 hashtags per post". Mosseri's top signals of Jan 22, 2025 are confirmed (watch time, likes, sends). The researcher correctly says that comment-to-follower conversion is not quantified anywhere. The daily routine is practitioner logic, not an Instagram rule.

findings.claim: Collab posts, including with the competitor itself, are the fastest legitimate way to get in front of an existing niche audience. Trial Reels let a professional account test content on non-followers.
findings.detail: Collab posts appear on each co-author's profile and are distributed to each account's audience. Current reports say up to 5 invited collaborators (6 accounts total) (Buffer; InstantDM says this is current as of Oct 2026, citing the Help Center). Some sources conflict on the exact count (e.g., Planable says 3), so check in-app. Instagram's own 2021 'Introducing Collabs' blog URL returned 404, so the primary source was not retrieved. Trial Reels: launched to professional accounts on Dec 10, 2024 (TechCrunch); they are shown to non-followers first and not on your grid. 2026 eligibility reports conflict (200 vs 1,000 followers; no Meta primary source found), so check in-app.
findings.recommendation: Pitch the competitor a non-zero-sum joint post: e.g., a Turkish/English co-production on one event (Çimpe 1352, 1877-78 muhaceret, 1912 Balkan Wars), each side bringing archival material. Also pitch muhacir/mübadil associations, Balkan Turkish cultural foundations, local-history and genealogy pages, and Balkan-origin creators. Offer to do the research and design work (you already have the post templates). Check whether Trial Reels are available on the new account and use them to test hooks.
findings.verify_note: TechCrunch (Dec 10, 2024, Aisha Malik) is confirmed word for word. The Buffer article is dated Jul 2, 2025, not undated, and says up to five. The researcher's '200 vs 1,000' conflict: the cited postfa.st page mentions only 1,000 and does not mention 200, so the source for 200 was not shown. postfa.st cites no Meta document. Its Trial Reels requirement is secondary and should be checked in the app, but the practical guidance changes from 'test hooks with Trial Reels' to 'probably unavailable until about 1,000 followers'.
findings.corrected_claim: Collab posts can include up to 5 collaborators besides the author, for 6 accounts in total. InstantDM (Oct 9, 2026) cites the Help Center: "You can add up to five collaborators to your post". The '3' figure comes from Meta's 2023 newsroom post and is outdated. Collabs work at any follower count (Buffer, Jul 2, 2025), but a private account can only invite accounts that follow it. Trial Reels launched on Dec 10, 2024 for professional accounts, are shown to non-followers, and do not appear on the grid. The only 2026 eligibility source found (postfa.st, updated Sep 20, 2026) says Trial Reels need a public professional account with at least 1,000 followers, and that 'New accounts and accounts under 1,000 followers do not have access'. A page launching on 2026-11-04 should therefore not count on Trial Reels at launch.

findings.claim: Comment-to-DM automation is allowed only through Meta's official API (Private Replies). It is limited to one message per commenter within 7 days, and gating content behind engagement can collide with Meta's spam policy wording.
findings.detail: Meta developer docs (Instagram Platform – Private Replies; listed as updated Jun 30, 2026 in search snippets): "Only one message can be sent to the commenter"; it "must be sent within 7 days"; follow-ups "only if the recipient responds, and must be sent within 24 hours". The reply lands in Inbox if the person follows you, otherwise in Requests. ManyChat says it is an official Meta Business Partner using official APIs; I did not verify this against Meta's partner directory. ManyChat community threads report that soft messaging restrictions can silently break comment-to-DM flows. Caution: Meta's Spam policy bars "Requiring users to engage (in the form of likes, shares, follows, or any other public-facing form of engagement)" before they can access content. A comment is public-facing engagement, so a hard 'comment to unlock' design is a grey area even though the API exists. Making 'follow me' a condition is clearly riskier.
findings.recommendation: Optional, after week 2: run 'comment KÖY and I'll DM you the 1912 map of your family's region' through an API-based tool that uses official Facebook/Instagram login (never a password). Keep the same resource also reachable without commenting (link in bio or highlight), never require a follow, and use it on a few posts, not all of them.
sources: https://developers.facebook.com/docs/instagram-platform/private-replies/ (Meta developer docs; updated Jun 30, 2026 per snippet)
findings.verify_note: Meta's Private Replies documentation, word for word: "Only one message can be sent to the commenter", "The message must be sent within 7 days of the comment was made on the post or reel", and "Follow-up messages can only be sent if the recipient responds, and must be sent within 24 hours of the response". The reply lands in the Inbox if the person follows the account, otherwise in Requests. The 'updated Jun 30, 2026' date did not appear in the fetched page content, so it is unverified. The Spam policy quote "Requiring users to engage (in the form of likes, shares, follows, or any other public-facing form of engagement)" does exist, in a 'Like/share-gating' sub-bullet under deceptive or misleading links. A separate bullet reads "Requiring or claiming that users are required to engage with content (e.g., liking, sharing) before they are able to view or interact with promised content." ManyChat's Meta Business Partner status is ManyChat's own claim, repeated by getkanal (updated Oct 12, 2026), and I did not check it independently.

findings.claim: Engagement pods, bought followers or likes, and follow-for-follow groups ('takip=takip', GT/DM groups, Telegram panels) are explicitly against Meta policy and can make the whole account non-recommendable. Bought or bot followers also get purged.
findings.detail: Meta Spam policy bans "selling, buying, or exchanging for engagement, such as likes, shares, views, follows" (this covers follow-for-follow groups and purchased followers). Instagram's recommendations guidelines exclude accounts that "Repeatedly engaged in misleading practices to build followings, such as purchasing 'likes'" and content boosted by "coordinated comment networks" (pods). Instagram removed large numbers of bot and long-inactive accounts in early May 2026 (widely reported as the 'Great Purge of 2026'), so bought followers can vanish. Mosseri reportedly warned against buying followers in a June 2021 Creators Q&A (secondhand, Digital Information World). Bought or bot followers never like or send, so they push down the per-viewer engagement Mosseri says matters (P6).
findings.recommendation: Zero tolerance: do not buy followers, likes or views (including Turkish 'takipçi satın al' panels), do not join pods or 'destek grupları', and do not run follow-for-follow. Real cross-promotion with peers (Collabs, genuine shout-outs) is fine. Mechanical exchange schemes are not.
findings.verify_note: The 'widely reported as the Great Purge of 2026' label could not be confirmed from the cited source. My web search was unavailable, so I could not test whether other outlets use it. The timing (early May 2026) agrees with Gulf News (May 7) and whatson.ae (May 14, 'happened very quickly this week'). The Mosseri 2021 item is secondhand, as the researcher said, and has no quote. The researcher left out one policy detail: the same Spam policy explicitly bans "Offering giveaways... of cash or cash equivalents in exchange for engagement".
findings.corrected_claim: The policy points are confirmed: Meta's Spam policy bans buying, selling or exchanging engagement, and Instagram's recommendations guidelines exclude misleading follower-building and coordinated comment networks. The supporting details were not confirmed by the cited sources. Gulf News (last updated May 7, 2026) reports Instagram removing millions of bot and inactive followers but does not use the term 'Great Purge' and quotes no Instagram executive. Digital Information World (Jun 12, 2021) reports only that Mosseri 'warned all users against... buying followers' and gives no direct quote.

findings.claim: 'Follow + tag 3 friends to win' giveaways are a legal risk in Turkey, apart from any platform issue. Any çekiliş needs Milli Piyango İdaresi permission, and the Finance Minister stated in January 2025 that unauthorized ones carry 3-6 years in prison plus a judicial fine.
findings.detail: Ekonomist (Jan 26, 2025, updated Jan 27, 2025) quotes Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek: "bedelli ya da bedelsiz her türlü eşya piyangosu veya çekiliş düzenlenmesi için izin alınması zorunludur", and unauthorized ones are "3 yıldan 6 yıla kadar hapis ile adli para cezası gerektiren bir suçtur". Turkish outlets reported in 2025 that the Istanbul prosecutor's office called 16 influencers to testify over unauthorized giveaways. Some Turkish legal blogs describe exceptions (e.g., certain social-purpose lotteries) and the sources do not fully agree, so this needs a legal check. On the platform side, Instagram's Promotion Guidelines (per third-party summaries; official page not retrieved) require official rules and a release of Instagram, and summaries conflict on whether 'follow to enter' is allowed. Meta's spam policy bars requiring follows to access promised content. Giveaway entrants are also mostly prize-seekers who unfollow afterwards (reasoning).
findings.recommendation: No giveaways at launch. If you ever run one, get MPİ permission or a lawyer's opinion first, do not make 'follow' a condition, and give a prize that only your real target audience values (e.g., a reprint of a historical map or a book on Rumeli history), so you attract the right people.
sources: https://www.ensonhaber.com/gundem/milli-piyangodan-izinsiz-cekilis-yapan-16-fenomene-sorusturma (2025; page returned 403, relied on search snippet)
findings.verify_note: The Ekonomist quotes are verbatim. The hukukihaber article is not undated: it is by Av. Nurdan Peksak, published 07.01.2021 and updated 27.12.2022. It cites the MPİ regulation as 'dated 4.10.2016, Resmi Gazete no. 26309'. That Gazette number appears to correspond to 2006, so check the date. It does not cite a specific law number for the prison penalty. I retrieved the official Promotion Guidelines (facebook.com/help/instagram/179379842258600), so the researcher's note that they were 'not retrieved' is now resolved. ensonhaber returned 403 again, so the 16-influencer report remains unverified. The core advice (no giveaways at launch; get legal or MPİ clearance first) still stands.
findings.corrected_claim: Ekonomist (Jan 26, 2025, updated Jan 27, 2025) quotes Minister Şimşek as saying that every 'eşya piyangosu veya çekiliş', paid or free, needs Milli Piyango İdaresi permission, and that running one without permission is 'a crime carrying 3 to 6 years in prison plus a judicial fine'. The MPİ regulation described by legal commentary does contain exceptions. These include skill-based contests and quizzes (yarışma/bilgi yarışması), prizes below a low value threshold (141.2 TL as of 2020, per the article), and social-purpose raffles run by public bodies. Permission requires a letter of guarantee (teminat mektubu) worth 110% of the prizes' market value. The report that 16 influencers were investigated could not be verified (the source returns HTTP 403). Instagram's official Promotion Guidelines require official rules, a complete release of Instagram by each entrant, and no inaccurate tagging. They say nothing for or against requiring a follow.

findings.claim: If the user still wants to follow people, a safe protocol is: manual only, warm targets only (recent active commenters), interact before following, a small daily cap that ramps slowly, no mass unfollowing, and stop at the first warning.
findings.detail: This protocol is my synthesis of P2-P13; it is not an Instagram-published rule. Prerequisites before the first follow: Professional/Creator account, finished bio, profile photo (the seal logo), 9-12 posts plus 2-3 highlights, so a visitor who checks you out has a reason to follow back. Ramp: days 1-7 at 0-10 follows/day; weeks 2-4 at 15-25/day; month 2+ at no more than 30-40/day if there have been no warnings. Pace: at most about 10 per hour, in 3-4 sessions with gaps, inside the official app on your usual device and network. Target only people who commented substantively on Rumeli/Balkan history posts (competitor's and others') in the last 2-4 weeks. Before following, like 1-2 of their posts or reply to their comment. Unfollowing: avoid it. If you must, wait at least 7-14 days, keep it at or below the same daily rate, and never bulk-unfollow. Keep total following under about 1,000. Stop rules: any 'Try again later' / 'We limit how often…' message means a 48-72 h full pause and then half the previous rate; check Account Status weekly. Measure follow-back percentage and, more importantly, whether those people engage afterwards.
findings.recommendation: Adopt this as the only acceptable version of the follow tactic and give it at most about 20% of daily growth time. Give the other 80% to content, comments (P10) and collabs (P11).
findings.verify_note: The researcher calls this protocol their own synthesis, and no official Instagram source backs it. Its numbers are internally consistent with the third-party estimates. Ramping to 15-25 follows a day, then 30-40, and keeping to 10 or fewer an hour sits inside SocialRails' 20-60 a day for new accounts and below Unfollr's halved figure of 25-50 a day for accounts under 6 months. Both sources say their figures are not official. The '48-72 h pause then half rate' rule and the 'under about 1,000 following' cap are heuristics with no source. Nothing found contradicts the protocol.

missed_points: How I checked: the shared WebSearch budget was already used up by the time of my first query, so every check above was done by opening the researcher's cited pages directly with WebFetch or curl. I could not search for independent alternative sources, and I could not check the competitor account: instagram.com returned HTTP 429, and third-party Instagram viewers are off-limits. I also could not check the 16-influencer report, because ensonhaber returned 403.

Meta's Spam policy explicitly bans "Offering giveaways (i.e., offering others a chance to win) of cash or cash equivalents in exchange for engagement" (example: "Anyone that likes my page will be entered to win $500"). It also bans "Offering to provide anything of monetary value in exchange for engagement". So a 'follow/like to win' giveaway with a cash or gift-card prize breaks platform policy on its own, separately from Turkish law. https://transparency.meta.com/policies/community-standards/spam/

Instagram's official Promotion Guidelines (retrieved via https://www.facebook.com/help/instagram/179379842258600) make the organizer responsible for the lawful operation of the promotion. They require official rules and "A complete release of Instagram by each entrant or participant", and they say "You must not inaccurately tag content or encourage users to inaccurately tag content." They say nothing about follow-to-enter.

Turkish raffle procedure, per Av. Nurdan Peksak on hukukihaber (published 07.01.2021, updated 27.12.2022): MPİ permission requires a letter of guarantee (teminat mektubu) worth 110% of the prizes' market value. The application goes to MPİ's Bahisler ve Oyunlar Şube Müdürlüğü, which should decide within 15 days. Skill-based contests and quizzes are listed as an exception, which could matter if the page later runs a Rumeli history quiz with a book prize. This still needs legal confirmation. https://www.hukukihaber.net/sosyal-medyada-yapilan-cekilisler-yasal-midir-belirli-bir-yaptirimi-mevcut-mudur

Trial Reels are probably not available to a brand-new account. postfa.st (updated Sep 20, 2026) says they need a public Creator or Business account with at least 1,000 followers, and that 'New accounts and accounts under 1,000 followers do not have access'. That source is secondary and cites no Meta document. For launch, the user should rely on the normal first test of every Reel on a small audience that includes non-followers (Instagram via Engadget, Apr 30, 2024). https://postfa.st/blog/instagram-trial-reels ; https://www.engadget.com/instagrams-algorithm-overhaul-will-reward-original-content-and-penalize-aggregators-130018977.html

Collabs do not require a minimum follower count (Buffer, Jul 2, 2025). However, a private account can only invite accounts that follow it, and if the original poster is private, only that account's followers see the post. The new page should therefore be public from day 1 to get the most out of Collabs. https://buffer.com/resources/instagram-collab-post/ ; https://instantdm.com/blog/instagram-collab-post (Oct 9, 2026)

Swapping mass follows for mass DMs to the competitor's followers carries the same spam risk. Metricool (Jan 21, 2026) estimates about 20-50 DMs a day for new accounts; this is an unofficial figure. Meta's spam policy targets high-frequency engagement whether it is manual or automated. https://metricool.com/instagram-limits/

Business Today (Dec 19, 2025) says the hashtag cap fell from 30 to 5, and that some users briefly saw a cap of 3 in testing. It says Instagram now weighs caption keywords, on-screen text and visuals more heavily than hashtags. For a Turkish history page, that supports putting place and event names (Rumeli, muhacir, 93 Harbi, Balkan Savaşı, Batı Trakya, and so on) in captions and on-screen text. https://www.businesstoday.in/technology/news/story/no-more-hashtag-stuffing-instagram-limits-hashtag-usage-to-just-5-per-reel-and-post-507444-2025-12-19

Unfollr (Jun 6, 2026, unofficial) says repeated follow-limit violations can escalate to blocks lasting 48 hours to a week that may require identity verification. A new account that has not yet set up verification details (phone or email) is more exposed to that. https://www.unfollr.com/blog/instagram-follow-unfollow-limits

Instagram's official Help Center pages are JS-rendered; the 7,500 cap, recommendations-eligibility and Terms texts were read via facebook.com/help/instagram mirrors on 2026-11-03, and the official Promotion Guidelines page and 'Introducing Collabs' blog were not retrieved.

summary: I could not find "Shadows of Rumelia" on any platform the web indexes, under any spelling. Instagram returned HTTP 429 or a login redirect, and the third-party viewer refused the request (403). So I have no data on the competitor. The user has to open that profile by hand. The online Balkan-Turk space in Turkish is busy but split up. The biggest Instagram accounts I could verify are about identity and community, not history: @bulgaristanturkleri (~138K), the official account of TRT1's Balkan Ninnisi series (~29K), @makedonyaturkleri (~20K) and @muhacirlercom (~20K). Association accounts sit between 1K and 11K (BAL-GÖÇ ~11K, Bosna Sancak Pendik ~9K, Rumeli Türkleri Kültür ve Dayanışma Derneği ~5K). These counts come from search-engine snapshots of unknown date. YouTube shows the clearest gap. Every Rumeli-specific channel has under 2K subscribers (Rumeli TV 1.66K). General Turkish history channels have hundreds of thousands to over a million (Harp Tarihi 880K, DFT Tarih 1.07M, Kronik Tarih 568K). Videos about mübadele and family stories regularly reach 50K–120K views. So I found no large Turkish-language page covering Ottoman Rumeli history from 1352 to 1912, which is exactly the slot "560 Yıl Rumeli" wants to fill. The offline community is dense and organized, which makes it the best route to fast organic growth. It includes federations (one had 85 member associations in 2018), BAL-GÖÇ (Bursa, 10 branches), BTTDD (13 branches in 2016), and the Lozan Mübadilleri Vakfı, which issued a joint statement with 30 other associations on 30 Jan 2026. It also includes museums in Edirne, Bursa and Çatalca, and the Time Balkan news site. Geographically, TÜİK 2022 counts 444,172 Balkan-born residents: 29.7% in Istanbul, 25.4% in Bursa, 13.3% in İzmir and 76.3% in the Marmara region overall. Descendants number in the many millions, but the 27–32M figures come from advocacy groups. On platforms, Instagram reaches about 71% of Turkey, YouTube about 78% and Facebook still about 35M people. The largest Balkan-migrant Facebook group I found is the main hub for nostalgia and identity posts. I found no reliable age breakdown by platform for this group.

findings.claim: I could not verify the 'Shadows of Rumelia' account on Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, X or Facebook, under any spelling. Its follower count, language, formats and posting frequency are all unknown to me.
findings.detail: Searched on 2026-11-03/04 with WebSearch: "Shadows of Rumelia" (standard and extended), shadowsofrumelia, shadows.of.rumelia, shadows_of_rumelia, 'Rumeli'nin Gölgeleri', 'Shadows of Rumeli', and the same with tiktok/youtube/facebook. All returned only Wikipedia pages about the region. Instagram profile URLs returned HTTP 429 or a 302 login redirect. The picuki viewer redirected to tikvib, which returned 403. A YouTube search for 'shadows of rumelia' found no matching channel. The user's figure of ~8000 followers is unverified. The English name suggests an English or bilingual page, but that is a guess.
findings.recommendation: The user should open the competitor profile while logged in and record a few things before launch: follower count, number of posts, posts per week, the top 9 posts by comments, the accounts that comment most, and the accounts it tags or collaborates with. The regular commenters (often tens to a few hundred people) are the warm audience. Engaging with them one by one through comments and replies, plus approaching the hubs listed below, should beat mass-following all 8,000. (My reasoning: blind mass-follow brings low follow-back rates, looks spammy and risks Instagram limits.)
sources: no source; searches returned no matching account (reasoning for the recommendation)
findings.verify_note: I could not search again: every WebSearch call came back with 'web search budget used up (limit 200 per turn)'. I fetched Instagram directly and got HTTP 429. A direct curl to Instagram was blocked by the sandbox's bot-check rule, and I did not try to get around it. So I can neither confirm nor refute that 'Shadows of Rumelia' exists or has ~8,000 followers. The advice to study commenters instead of mass-following is reasoning, not a sourced platform rule. I could not check Instagram's 2025–2026 follow or action limits.

findings.claim: The largest Balkan-Turk Instagram accounts I could verify are identity and community pages, not history pages. I found no sizeable Turkish-language Instagram page on Ottoman Rumeli history.
findings.detail: From search-engine snapshots of Instagram profiles (dates unknown, so treat as approximate): @bulgaristanturkleri ~138K followers / 717 posts; @balkanninnisitrt, the official TRT1 series account, ~29K / 1,178 posts; @makedonyaturkleri ~20K / 713 posts; @muhacirlercom 'Balkan Muhacirleri' (bio: a meeting place for Balkan Turks) ~20K / 484 posts; @rumelia.tr (Rumelia Qulture culture magazine) ~2.3K.
findings.recommendation: Treat these as distribution partners, not rivals. Pitch each one a co-authored post (Instagram Collab feature) or a story share of a carousel tied to their region, for example a 'Üsküp 1392–1912' piece for @makedonyaturkleri or a Filibe/Kırcaali piece for @bulgaristanturkleri. Position 560 Yıl Rumeli as the history layer these identity pages are missing.
findings.verify_note: Instagram profile pages returned HTTP 429 to WebFetch, and direct access was blocked, so I could not check any follower or post count (138K, 29K, 20K, 20K, 2.3K). They should stay labelled as search-snapshot numbers of unknown date. The user should check them while logged in before naming them anywhere.

findings.claim: Instagram accounts of associations and clubs make a ready list of local hubs with roughly 1K–11K followers each, useful for reposts and collabs.
findings.detail: Snapshot counts: @balgocgenelmerkez (BAL-GÖÇ HQ) ~11K / 2,396 posts; @bosnasancakpendik1992 (Bosna Sancak Derneği, Istanbul Anatolian side) ~9.0K; @rumelidernegi1950 (Rumeli Türkleri Kültür ve Dayanışma Derneği) ~5.2K / 941 posts; @batitrakyaspor ~2.5K; @batitrakya_ ~1.4K; @birbalgoc (Birleşik Balkan Göçmenleri Der.) ~1.16K; @btkoyleri (Batı Trakya Köyleri) ~977. These accounts post often, which suggests they welcome outside content.
findings.recommendation: Follow and engage with these accounts on day one. Send each a short DM offering free, credited history content about their region or town, such as a carousel they can repost. Tag them in relevant posts. Associations also hold events, which are a chance for offline QR-code promotion.
findings.verify_note: Same Instagram block. Some parts do check out: balgoc.org.tr links to instagram.com/balgocgenelmerkez, and bttdd.org.tr links to facebook.com/bttdd and twitter.com/bttddgm. The follower counts (11K, 9.0K, 5.2K and so on) are unverified.

findings.claim: On YouTube, Rumeli and Balkan-Turk channels are tiny (all under ~2K subscribers), while general Turkish and Ottoman history channels have hundreds of thousands to over a million. There is no strong Rumeli history channel.
findings.detail: From YouTube channel search pages on 2026-11-03/04. Rumeli-specific: Rumeli TV 1.66K subscribers (joined Jan 2024, 46,921 total views); Balkan Türkleri 534; Türkiye ve Rumeli Evliyaları 528; Samsun Balkan Türkleri Derneği 408; Kuşadası Mübadele Evi 323; Time Balkan 757; Biz Rumeliyiz 122; RUMELİSİAD Bursa 67. General history: DFT Tarih 1.07M; Gerçeği Bul 1.03M; Harp Tarihi 880K; Tarih Obası 585K; Kronik Tarih 568K; OMNIBUS 507K; Tarih ve Türkler 210K; Osmanlı Tarihi 176K; Tarih 101 119K; Uyku ve Tarih 96.1K; Sancaray 60.3K; Kültür Tarihi 48.3K; Kör Tarih 29.5K (top result for 'rumeli tarihi'); Gündem Tarih 28.5K.
findings.recommendation: Reuse each Instagram Reel as a YouTube Short from day one, because the Rumeli history slot there is empty. Mid-size history channels (Kör Tarih, Gündem Tarih, Sancaray, Kültür Tarihi) are realistic first collaboration or guest-research targets. The 500K+ channels are later targets once the page has proof of traction.
findings.verify_note: I fetched each YouTube channel page directly on 2026-11-04. All counts matched exactly: Rumeli TV 1.66K (joined 18 Jan 2024; 46,930 total views now against the researcher's 46,921), Balkan Türkleri 534, Kuşadası Mübadele Evi 323, Time Balkan 757, Harp Tarihi 880K, DFT Tarih 1.07M, Kronik Tarih 568K, Tarih Obası 585K, Tarih ve Türkler 210K, Osmanlı Tarihi 176K, Sancaray 60.3K, Kör Tarih 29.5K, Gündem Tarih 28.5K. One addition: BAL-GÖÇ's channel (@balgocgenelmerkez8980) has 700. I did not check the channels without a URL (Gerçeği Bul, OMNIBUS, Tarih 101 and others), and I could not test the claim that Kör Tarih is the top result for 'rumeli tarihi'. 'All Rumeli channels under 2K' only holds for the channels found.

findings.claim: Videos about mübadele and personal migration stories reliably get tens of thousands of views on YouTube in Turkish. The memory of families and journeys is what gets watched.
findings.detail: Views from YouTube search on 2026-11-03: T24 'Kayıp bir kuşağın hikâyesi Mübadele' 121,386; +90 'Acı göç: Mübadele' 116,372; Can Ertuna '90 Yıllık Ayrılık Mübadele' 91,373; Konak Belediyesi 'Mübadele 100 Yıllık Hasret' 57,587; the Lozan Mübadilleri Vakfı channel's 'mübadele belgeseli' 50,175; Trakya ve Işıklar Köyü Selanikliler Derneği 'Selanik'ten Tekirdağ'a' 15,085 (9 months old). In English, The Great War's 'The Balkan Wars 1912-1913' has 2.81M views.
findings.recommendation: Add a recurring format that links each period of 1352–1912 to the follower's own family. Examples: 'Deden hangi sancaktan?' maps, town-of-origin carousels, and a call to followers to send family photos and stories that the page can retell. User-submitted stories also get shared inside family WhatsApp groups.
findings.verify_note: Every view count comes from a YouTube search results page. With the search budget gone, I did not query YouTube search as a substitute. None of the individual figures (121,386; 116,372; 91,373; 57,587; 50,175; 15,085; 2.81M) could be checked. The pattern (mübadele and family stories draw views) is plausible but unconfirmed here.

findings.claim: The largest Balkan-migrant hub I found is a Facebook group. A 2025 academic study of its 517 posts found the main themes were nostalgia and collective memory, identity, and ties across borders.
findings.detail: Ünügür, 5th International Balkan Studies Congress (Skopje, 5–7 Sep 2025), proceedings pp. 601–614. The group 'Selanik, Rumeli ve Balkan Göçmenleri – Thessaloniki, Rumelia and Balkan Migrants' is described as having 'the largest membership among similar groups'; no member count is given. Theme shares: nostalgia/collective memory 32.2%, identity representation 28%, transnational ties 22.1%. Separately, the BTTDD HQ Facebook page shows ~8,008 likes.
findings.recommendation: Join the large muhacir and mübadil Facebook groups as a person, and share posts natively, without spammy links. Follow each group's rules and lead with nostalgia and identity angles. Older community members appear to gather on Facebook (an inference from where the hubs are), so Facebook is the bridge to the elders who share content with younger relatives.
findings.verify_note: The Avesis record matches: Ünügür N. A., 5th International Balkan Studies Congress, Üsküp, 5–7 Sep 2025, pp. 601–614, 517 posts from the previous 12 months, group 'Selanik, Rumeli ve Balkan Göçmenleri – Thessaloniki, Rumelia and Balkan Migrants', themes 32.2% / 28% / 22.1%. It gives no member count, only the relative phrase 'largest membership among similar groups'. The ~8,008 likes on BTTDD's Facebook page could not be checked (login wall). The claim that elders gather on Facebook is still an inference.

findings.claim: Umbrella organizations (federations and a confederation) connect dozens of local Rumeli and Balkan associations. One partnership can reach many groups at once.
findings.detail: Rumeli Balkan Dernekleri Federasyonu: founded 2006, 85 member associations and HQ moved to Bayrampaşa (Istanbul), per a 31 May 2018 report; its president then claimed more than 30M Rumelis in Turkey. Ege Balkan Rumeli Dernekleri Federasyonu (İzmir) had ~40,000 members in 2012. Balkan Rumeli Türkleri Konfederasyonu was active in 2022 (urging dual citizens to vote in Bulgaria). Trakya Rumeli Balkan Dernekleri Federasyonu (TRAKYA RUBAFED) runs trakyarubafed.com. Rumeli Türk Dernekleri Federasyonu (2016, president Kerim Erden) included BTTDD and Bosna Sancak groups. The Balkan Rumeli Dernekleri iftar on 11 Mar 2026 at Eyüpsultan drew the CHP leader, showing how visible these groups are.
findings.recommendation: Write a one-page media kit about the page's mission and send it to federation press offices. Offer a weekly 'Rumeli tarihinde bu hafta' post they can share or put in newsletters. Ask to be introduced to member associations' social media managers.
findings.verify_note: I opened every source except trakyarubafed.com. The main correction is the 'more than 30M' wording. Another umbrella body was missed: Karadeniz Rumeli Dernekleri Federasyonu signed the 30 Jan 2026 statement.
findings.corrected_claim: Rumeli Balkan Dernekleri Federasyonu (founded 2006) said in a 31 May 2018 report that it was the umbrella for 85 associations and had moved its HQ to Bayrampaşa. Its president, Kamuran Atakan, claimed 'about 30 million' (30 milyon civarında) Rumelis in Turkey, not 'more than 30M'. Ege Balkan Rumeli Dernekleri Federasyonu had 'close to 40,000' members (3 Oct 2012). Balkan Rumeli Türkleri Konfederasyonu urged dual citizens to vote in Bulgaria's election (BTA, 10 Sep 2022). In Feb 2016, Rumeli Türk Dernekleri Federasyonu (president Kerim Erden) was made up of three associations. From the text, these are Bosna Sancak Kültür ve Yardımlaşma Derneği, Göçmenlere Yardım Derneği and BTTDD (whose chairman was a federation deputy chairman). The Balkan Rumeli Dernekleri iftar on 11 Mar 2026 at Eyüpsultan Kültür Sanat Merkezi was attended by CHP leader Özgür Özel. The article does not name an organizing federation.

findings.claim: BAL-GÖÇ (Balkan Göçmenleri Kültür ve Dayanışma Derneği) is based in Bursa, lists 10 branches and runs official Instagram, Facebook, X and YouTube accounts.
findings.detail: balgoc.org.tr lists branches in Bandırma, Görükle, İnegöl, İznik, Karacabey, Kestel, Mustafakemalpaşa, Orhangazi, Osmangazi and Yenişehir. Socials: instagram.com/balgocgenelmerkez (~11K), facebook.com/BalgocGenelMerkez, twitter.com/bursabalgoc, youtube.com/@balgocgenelmerkez8980. A 2012 report described an İzmir-based association of the same name with 7 branches and ~15,000 members. It may be a separate registered body; I could not confirm.
findings.recommendation: BAL-GÖÇ is the top target in Bursa, which holds the second-largest Balkan-born population. Offer content for its anniversaries and galas. Its website also has a 'Balkanların Tarihçesi' section, a natural opening for a content partnership.
findings.verify_note: balgoc.org.tr lists exactly these 10 branches: Bandırma, Görükle, İnegöl, İznik, Karacabey, Kestel, Mustafakemalpaşa, Orhangazi, Osmangazi, Yenişehir. It links the stated Instagram, Facebook, X (bursabalgoc) and YouTube accounts. The site never names its HQ city. Bursa is inferred from the 224 area code and the 'bursabalgoc' handle. The YouTube channel has 700 subscribers. The 2012 Mynet article does describe an İzmir-based 'Balkan Göçmenleri Kültür ve Dayanışma Derneği' with 7 branches and 15,000 members. Whether it is the same legal body is still unknown. The ~11K Instagram count was not checked.

findings.claim: The Western Thrace network is well organized in Turkey and in Europe: BTTDD in Turkey, ABTTF in Germany and Belgium, and the Millet news outlet in Xanthi.
findings.detail: BTTDD was founded in 1946. In 2016 it had its HQ, 13 branches, 4 representative offices, 2 foundations and 2 sports clubs; branches mentioned include İzmir, Edremit, Keşan and Bursa. Website bttdd.org.tr; Facebook ~8K likes. ABTTF (Avrupa Batı Trakya Türk Federasyonu) was founded 28 Feb 1988 in Giessen, has its HQ in Witten (Germany), a Brussels office and FUEN membership. Millet (milletnews.com, Millet Media, Xanthi, English-language) covers BTTDD activity (e.g. Keşan branch visit, article dated 20 Feb 2026).
findings.recommendation: Make a Western Thrace history series (Gümülcine, İskeçe, Dimetoka under Ottoman rule) and offer it to BTTDD and ABTTF. ABTTF also opens a route to the diaspora in Germany and Europe.
findings.verify_note: The branch list 'İzmir, Edremit, Keşan, Bursa' is not supported by the cited 2016 article. ABTTF's Brussels office, its FUEN membership and the ~8K Facebook likes were not verified.
findings.corrected_claim: BTTDD's 2026 website carries the headline 'BATI TRAKYA TÜRKLERİ DAYANIŞMA DERNEĞİ 80 YAŞINDA', which fits a 1946 founding. In Feb 2016 it had its HQ, 13 branches, 4 representative offices, 2 foundations and 2 sports clubs (Time Balkan). The 2016 article names no branch cities. The current site mentions İzmit and Zeytinburnu branches, and a Keşan branch is confirmed by Millet. ABTTF's letterhead reads 'Kuruluş/Gegr. 28.02.1988, VR 1954, Giessen', with its address in Witten. Millet (Millet Media, Xanthi) published an English article dated 20 Feb 2026 on the BTTDD Keşan branch's visit to Gümülcine and İskeçe.

findings.claim: The mübadele network acts as a coalition. On 30 Jan 2026 the Lozan Mübadilleri Vakfı and 30 other associations issued a joint statement for the 103rd anniversary of the exchange, and the network runs museums and 'Mübadele Evi' houses.
findings.detail: Signatories are based in Bursa, Samsun, Sinop, Gemlik, Gelibolu, Mudanya, Erdek, Çatalca, Bodrum, Kuşadası, Çukurova, and several districts of İzmir and Istanbul. The Çatalca Mübadele Müzesi opened in Dec 2010, set up by the Lozan Mübadilleri Vakfı, the Istanbul 2010 agency and Çatalca Municipality. Bursa Lozan Mübadilleri opened a Mübadele Evi. Kuşadası Mübadele Evi has a YouTube channel. The foundation's website could not be reached (503).
findings.recommendation: 30 January is a yearly peak for this community. Although 1923 falls outside 1352–1912, a 'before the exchange: Ottoman Selanik/Kavala/Drama' series published around 30 Jan could be shared across all 31 organizations. Pitch it to the foundation's coordinators in early January.
findings.verify_note: Kent ve Bellek, 30 Jan 2026, 19:45: 31 organizations signed, with Lozan Mübadilleri Vakfı at no. 18. So 'the Vakıf plus 30 others' is right. Not all signatories are Rumeli associations, though. The list includes a research center (Asya Balkan Stratejik Araştırmalar Merkezi Derneği), a federation (Karadeniz Rumeli Dernekleri Federasyonu), several Lozan Mübadilleri regional offices, and Cretan groups (Çukurova Girit Mübadilleri, İstanbul Giritliler, Bodrum Girit ve Yunanistan Göçmenleri). The Çatalca museum's Dec 2010 opening (benguturk returned 403) and the Bursa Mübadele Evi (Medium returned 403) were not verified. Kuşadası Mübadele Evi's YouTube channel exists, with 323 subscribers.

findings.claim: Time Balkan is a Turkish-language Balkan news site that already runs a 'Balkanlar Tarihinde Bugün' feature. Its social accounts are a direct overlap and a possible amplifier.
findings.detail: timebalkan.com has sections for each Balkan country and history items, for example Yahya Kemal's journey from Üsküp to Istanbul, with headlines from Nov 2026. Socials: instagram.com/time_balkan (follower count not found), twitter.com/timebalkan_, facebook.com/timebalkan, and a YouTube channel with ~757 subscribers. Also in the space: muhacirler.com ('Balkan Türklerini Buluşturan Platform', Istanbul; publishes Balkan Günlüğü issues and lists 21 associations) and the Rumelia Qulture magazine (@rumelia.tr).
findings.recommendation: Pitch Time Balkan and muhacirler.com a weekly short history column, or let them embed the page's carousels, with credit and the handle. Earned media like this brings followers who already care about the topic.
findings.verify_note: The researcher's tagline 'Balkan Türklerini Buluşturan Platform' does not match the current page, and '21 associations listed' is really just a counter. Time Balkan's Instagram follower count was not found. Because Time Balkan already runs a daily history feature, the claim that nobody covers Rumeli history is weaker than stated.
findings.corrected_claim: timebalkan.com has a 'BALKANLAR Tarihinde Bugün' section, including an undated piece titled 'Üsküp'te Başlayan Bir Ruhun İstanbul'a Yolculuğu: Yahya Kemal Beyatlı'. Its news headlines are dated 1–3 Nov 2026. It links instagram.com/time_balkan, twitter.com/timebalkan_, facebook.com/timebalkan and a YouTube channel (@timebalkan2101, 757 subscribers). muhacirler.com now calls itself 'Balkan Türklerinin Platformu' and is run by Balkan Türkleri Cemiyeti (Istanbul). It shows a counter of 21 STKs, with no list on the page, and lists Balkan Günlüğü issues such as 710, 711 and 716.

findings.claim: Academic partners who can add credibility exist: Trakya University's Balkan Araştırma Enstitüsü and İstanbul Rumeli University's Rumeli research center (RUÇAM). Standard authors on Rumeli migration are also easy to name.
findings.detail: Trakya Üniversitesi Balkan Araştırma Enstitüsü was founded in 2011 (Edirne) and publishes BAED twice a year (indexed in ESCI and TR Dizin). İstanbul Rumeli Üniversitesi RUÇAM, directed by Dr. Erdem Eren, publishes the 'Rumelian Media Report' (Issue 3, April 2026). There is also the Rumeli İslâm Araştırmaları Dergisi (Trakya-region theology faculties). Key texts: Bilal Şimşir, 'Rumeli'den Türk Göçleri' (1989), Hasip Saygılı, 'Rumeli'de Bizden Ne Kaldı?', and Taha Akyol's YouTube documentary playlist 'Rumeli'ye Elveda: 100. Yılında Balkan Bozgunu'.
findings.recommendation: Ask one or two academics, for example graduate students at BAE or RUÇAM, to fact-check or guest-explain monthly. Use an 'akademik danışman' credit. It protects credibility, gives them a reason to share, and academic institutions repost content they took part in.
findings.verify_note: The RUÇAM PDF title page reads 'Rumelian Media Report – Issue 3, April 2026', with editor Dr. Erdem EREN, Assistant Professor and Director of RUÇAM. The DergiPark page confirms that BAED is Trakya Üniversitesi Balkan Araştırma Enstitüsü's journal, published twice a year (July and December), indexed in ESCI and TR Dizin, and publishing since Dec 2012. The page does not confirm the institute's 2011 founding. The YouTube playlist title is 'Rumeli'ye Elveda: 100. Yılında Balkan Bozgunu (Belgesel)' and the page shows Taha Akyol. I did not check the Şimşir and Saygılı book details.

findings.claim: Museums and recurring events in Edirne and Bursa are offline places where this audience gathers and that can be geotagged.
findings.detail: Edirne: Balkan Tarihi Müzesi in the restored Hıdırlık Tabyası, and Şükrü Paşa Anıtı ve Balkan Savaşları Müzesi. Edirne Balkan Folklore Festival runs alongside Kırkpınar; the 3rd edition was in 2023. Bursa: Göç Tarihi Müzesi, run by the metropolitan municipality, which staged a Belene camp exhibition. The 13th International Balkan Countries Theatre Festival was held in Bursa on 3–12 April 2026, sited there because of the large Balkan-origin population. I found no mübadele house museum in Kırklareli; Kırklareli Müzesi is a general museum.
findings.recommendation: Shoot on-site Reels at these museums and geotag them, since location pages show posts to visitors. Tag the museum and municipality accounts and ask them to repost. Plan posts around the Bursa festival (April) and Kırkpınar (summer).
findings.verify_note: Two parts of the original are not in the cited sources: the festival being held in Bursa 'because of the large Balkan-origin population', and the folklore festival 'running alongside Kırkpınar'. The Belene exhibition dates from 2019, not recently. The Sygic and KHAS sources were not opened.
findings.corrected_claim: Hıdırlık Bastion in Edirne reopened as the 'Edirne Balkan History Museum' (Hurriyet Daily News, 1 Jan 2022). The museum presents '600 years of Turkish history in the Balkans' and the 155-day defence of 1913 under Şükrü Pasha. The 3rd Balkan Folklore Festival opened in Edirne in July 2023 (BTA, 2 Jul 2023). The article does not mention Kırkpınar. The 13th International Balkan Countries Theatre Festival ran in Bursa on 3–12 April 2026, but the source gives no reason for choosing Bursa. The Belene camp exhibition was staged by Bursa Metropolitan Municipality at the 'Bursa Göç Müzesi' in December 2019.

findings.claim: Turkey has 444,172 Balkan-born residents (TÜİK 2022). They are concentrated in Istanbul (29.7%), Bursa (25.4%) and İzmir (13.3%), with 76.3% in the Marmara region.
findings.detail: From Eşim & Zaman (2024), International Journal of Social Inquiry 17(2), using TÜİK ADNKS 2022: Istanbul 132,043; Bursa 112,863; İzmir 59,151; Tekirdağ 38,707; Kocaeli 16,046; Edirne 9,962; Kırklareli 9,434; Ankara 8,545; Manisa 8,335; Eskişehir 8,065; Balıkesir 5,604; Sakarya 4,704; Antalya 4,591; Yalova 4,542; Çanakkale 4,127. Other figures: Bulgaria-born people were the largest foreign-born group, at 11.4% of 3,141,351 in the 2021 census (≈358K, my calculation). In Bursa, 48.4% of foreign-born residents were Bulgaria-born (2019). Bayrampaşa (Istanbul) is often named as a district where many Rumeli migrants live. These counts cover first-generation residents only; descendants are far more numerous.
findings.recommendation: If the page runs any paid boosts, target Istanbul, Bursa, İzmir, Tekirdağ, Kocaeli, Edirne, Kırklareli, Manisa, Eskişehir and Balıkesir. Build early posts around towns these families came from, and use Istanbul, Bursa and İzmir locations for geotags.
findings.verify_note: I extracted the Eşim & Zaman (2024) PDF, IJSI 17(2), pp. 383–405. The text gives 444,172 Balkan-born residents in 2022 (TÜİK, Yurt Dışı Doğumlu Nüfus). Its Table 7 matches every provincial figure exactly: Istanbul 132,043 (29.7%), Bursa 112,863 (25.4%), İzmir 59,151 (13.3%), Tekirdağ 38,707 and so on. Its Table 8 gives Marmara 338,820 (76.3%). One small point: Edirne is 2.2% in the table and 2% in the text. The TÜİK 2021 release (via alomaliye) says that of 3,141,351 foreign-born residents, Bulgaria-born were first at 11.4%. Bursa's 48.4% Bulgaria-born figure (2019, ADNKS) is confirmed. The Özlem (2017) claim of more than 250K Turks moving from Bulgaria to the EU after 2001 appears in Eşim & Zaman.

findings.claim: Estimates of Turks with Balkan or Rumeli ancestry run from about 8.5M (descendants of post-1923 migrants) to 27–32M (including pre-1923 migration). The higher numbers come from an advocacy group's model.
findings.detail: Prof. Dr. Necdet Tekin for RUBASAM (Rumeli Balkan Center for Strategic Studies), 'Migrations from Rumelia and the Balkans... Forecasts for 2020': post-1923 migrants grown to 2020 = 8,464,016 (10.12% of 83.6M); total 27,641,388 (minimum) to 31,911,878 (maximum). The authors admit a simple two-variable growth model with uncertain inputs. A federation president claimed 'more than 30 million' (2018). Wikipedia-derived pages say 'a quarter to a third' of Turkey's population.
findings.recommendation: In public copy say 'milyonlarca Rumeli evladı' rather than quoting 30M as fact. Internally, the potential audience is in the millions, which supports the user's ambition.
findings.verify_note: Tekin's slides (PDF extracted) give Model A, post-1923 = 8,464,016 (10.12% of 83,614,362), a minimum total of 27,641,388 and a maximum of 31,911,878. They call the model 'mathematically and statistically simple and only bivariate'. They also say the error from uncertain source data 'was not possible to measure or estimate'. Tekin is described as a RUBASAM board member and a former Turkish Minister of National Education. The federation's 2018 claim should read 'about 30 million', not 'more than 30 million'. Low confidence is right; advising against quoting 30M as fact is sound.

findings.claim: There is a Turkish-speaking audience in the Balkans and in the European diaspora: about 508K Turks in Bulgaria, 19K in Kosovo, an estimated 100–210K in Western Thrace, plus Bulgarian Turks in the Netherlands, Germany and Sweden.
findings.detail: Bulgaria 2021 census: 508,375 Turks (Wikipedia; TR Wikipedia gives 508,378). Kosovo 2024 census: 19,419 Turks (1.21%), mostly in Prizren (9,819) and Mamuşa (5,220). Western Thrace: estimated 100,000–210,000 (Wikipedia). Netherlands: 10–30K people from Bulgaria, ~80% ethnic Turks mostly from Kırcaali (Wikipedia-derived). More than 250K Turks from Bulgaria moved to EU countries after 2001 (Özlem 2017, cited in Eşim & Zaman). I did not verify a North Macedonia 2021 census figure.
findings.recommendation: Write captions for people in Turkey and abroad alike, and add place names in their Balkan-language forms (Kardzhali/Kırcaali, Prizren/Prizren). Test posting times that suit Central European evenings. Reach diaspora associations through ABTTF and Bulgarian-Turk groups in the Netherlands.
findings.verify_note: English Wikipedia gives 508,375 Turks in Bulgaria's 2021 census in its lead and infobox, and a table total of 508,378. Kosovo's 2024 census: 19,419 Turks (1.2%), Prizren 9,819, Mamuşa 5,220 (93.09%). The Western Thrace infobox range of 100,000–210,000 is right, but the article body cites the 1991 Greek census at about 50,000 of Turkish origin and a wider Muslim community of 90,000–120,000. Treat 210K as a high-end estimate. The Netherlands figure of 10–30K is an uncited Wikipedia infobox estimate. findings.claim: In Turkey, Instagram and YouTube reach about 70–78% of people and Facebook about 35M. I found no breakdown by age per platform for Turkey or for Balkan-origin people.
findings.detail: TÜİK 2026 household IT survey (reported 5 Aug 2026, ages 16–74): WhatsApp 90.0%, YouTube 77.6%, Instagram 71.1%. DataReportal 'Digital 2026: Turkey' (published 8 Nov 2025, data from late 2025): Instagram ad reach 62.3M (70.9% of population; 92.1% of adults 18+), YouTube 57.9M (66.0%), TikTok 44.9M adults (68.6% of 18+), Facebook 34.7M (39.5%; 53.2% of adults; ad audience 64.4% male), X 18.5M. The common belief that older people use Facebook and younger people use Instagram/TikTok is not confirmed by these sources. It only fits indirectly with the fact that the largest muhacir hub is a Facebook group (N6).
findings.recommendation: Make Instagram the main platform. Cross-post Reels to YouTube Shorts and TikTok, and share to Facebook groups for older relatives. Add a 'WhatsApp'ta paylaş' prompt, since WhatsApp at 90% is where family chains forward content.
findings.verify_note: Haberler.com, 5 Aug 2026, reporting TÜİK's 2026 household IT survey (ages 16–74): internet use 92.3%, WhatsApp 90.0%, YouTube 77.6%, Instagram 71.1% (men 71.9%, women 70.2%).
