summary: The biggest legal trap is the classic "follow + tag 3 friends, we'll draw a winner" giveaway. In Turkey, a random-draw giveaway on social media needs prior permission from Milli Piyango İdaresi (MPİ) under its 2006 regulation on non-cash lotteries and draws. In January 2025 the Finance Minister warned that unauthorized draws carry 3 to 6 years in prison, and MPİ filed 286 criminal complaints in 2024. For a personal history page, the safe route is a contest judged on skill or by a jury, not a random draw. The biggest reach trap is unoriginal content. Instagram (April 2026, now covering photos and carousels too) and Facebook (July 2025) stop recommending accounts that mostly repost material they haven't meaningfully changed, and Reels carrying other apps' watermarks have been held back since 2021. Every archival photo therefore needs added value: original captions with sources, maps, voiceover. Following 8,000 competitor followers one by one breaks the spirit of Instagram's rule against artificially inflating followers. There's no published daily follow limit, so it risks action blocks, and the "follow-back" followers it brings in are low quality. Collab posts with muhacir associations (BAL-GÖÇ, verified: 10 branches across Bursa districts, active on Instagram, Facebook, X, YouTube and WhatsApp), academics and YouTubers are the safest organic shortcut. Paid ads in Turkey are cheap but there's no reliable benchmark: 2026 web sources put Meta CPM at roughly $2-5, and I found no trustworthy cost-per-follower figure. On top of the ad spend come Meta's 5% Turkey "location fee" (in effect by November 2026) and VAT (20% general rate, though not every source agrees). On risk: Instagram doesn't push "political content" by default, Balkan topics draw comment raids and mass-reporting, and photos of graphic atrocities or photorealistic AI images without a label make posts or whole accounts ineligible for recommendation. The same goes for repeated content rated false by fact-checkers. Doğruluk Payı runs a "Tarih ve Dezenformasyon" (History and Disinformation) series, so made-up quotes and misattributed photos can get publicly debunked. Account security means app-based two-factor authentication and ignoring DMs about "copyright violation" or a "blue badge": Instagram says it never DMs about copyright. Limitation: the web-search budget shared across this run ran out partway through. Some points (Facebook-group, Reddit and Ekşi norms, Collab feature details, music rules, mass-reporting mechanics) rely on direct page fetches or my own reasoning and are marked as such.

findings.claim: Random-draw social media giveaways (çekiliş) for promoting an account legally need prior permission from Milli Piyango İdaresi (MPİ) in Turkey. Unauthorized draws are prosecuted, and the Finance Minister said in January 2025 that the penalty is 3 to 6 years in prison plus a judicial fine.
findings.detail: Legal basis: 'Milli Piyango İdaresi Genel Müdürlüğü Karşılığı Nakit Olmayan Piyangolar ve Çekilişler Hakkında Yönetmelik', Resmi Gazete 4 Oct 2006, No. 26309. One law site prints the year as 2016, which looks like a typo for 2006. Article 7 requires prior permission for draws that promote an account or brand. Article 10 says a draw on a virtual platform must be tied to promoting or selling a good or service and cannot aim directly at generating income (Hukuki Haber, 7 Jan 2021, updated 27 Dec 2022). A permit needs a bank guarantee worth the prize value plus 10%, and the application is filed about 15 days ahead. Ekonomist, 26 Jan 2025: Minister Mehmet Şimşek warned specifically about unauthorized draws on social media. In his words, any goods draw, paid or free, needs MPİ permission, the penalty is '3 yıldan 6 yıla kadar hapis ile adli para cezası', and MPİ filed criminal complaints over 286 unauthorized draws and applications in 2024. In January 2021, Istanbul prosecutors investigated 10 influencers, including Enes Batur and Reynmen, for giveaways run without permission (Gazete Vatan, 12 Jan 2021). Permit fees on eleman.net (15 Oct 2025: about 500 / 3,500 / 6,000+ TL by prize value) are unofficial and look unreliable. The source does not name the legal article behind the 3-6 year penalty.
findings.recommendation: Do not run a 'follow, like, tag 3 friends, and we'll draw a winner' giveaway at launch. A personal (non-company) history page probably can't even fit Article 10's requirement to be tied to a product or service. If the user wants a prize campaign later, get a Turkish lawyer's opinion first, or go through a partner company or association that applies for an MPİ permit.
findings.verify_note: I checked each part of this. The regulation is the 'Nakit Olmayan Piyangolar ve Çekilişler Hakkında Yönetmelik', Resmi Gazete 4 Oct 2006, No. 26309 (on resmigazete.gov.tr). Hukuki Haber prints '4.10.2016', which is a typo. Art. 7(1) says anyone organising a piyango must apply to the İdare and get permission. It does not specifically mention 'account/brand promotion'; that phrasing is the researcher's gloss. Art. 10(1) confirmed: online draws must be based on promoting, selling or marketing a good or service, and draws aimed directly at income are not allowed. Art. 10(2) adds more online conditions: collect each entrant's name, address and a code, notify winners by registered mail, and submit participant data to the İdare before the draw. Ekonomist (26 Jan 2025, updated 27 Jan) confirmed Şimşek's quotes: '3 yıldan 6 yıla kadar hapis ile adli para cezası', 'bedelli ya da bedelsiz her türlü eşya piyangosu', 286 criminal complaints in 2024, and the social-media warning. Gazete Vatan (12 Jan 2021) confirmed that the Istanbul Chief Prosecutor investigated 10 influencers, including Enes Batur and Reynmen. That article gave the penalty as up to 2 years in prison and an administrative fine of up to 10M TL. So the penalty framing differs between 2021 and 2025, and the legal article behind '3-6 years' is still unidentified. The only penalty article Hukuki Haber cites is TCK 157 (fraud, for prizes that are never delivered). The 10%-over-prize-value guarantee is confirmed only by the İşbank blog (9 Feb 2023). The '15 days ahead' lead time does not appear in either the İşbank or eleman.net article, so it is unverified. The eleman.net fees (15 Oct 2025: 500 / 3,500 / 6,000+ TL) match what the researcher reported. The page itself calls them approximate and points to MPİ.

findings.claim: The regulation exempts skill- or jury-based competitions (yarışma), puzzles and very low-value prizes. That makes a judged contest the legal alternative to a random-draw giveaway.
findings.detail: According to Hukuki Haber, the exemptions are: competitions where prizes go on merit (knowledge, skill or talent) or by jury decision, plus riddles and puzzles; draws whose prize per person is below 2% of the amount in Law 7338 Art. 4(e) (141.2 TL in 2020; I could not verify the 2026 figure); social-purpose draws by public bodies; and selection draws with no prize. The article says the exact boundaries are open to interpretation.
findings.recommendation: Run a judged contest instead, for example 'Ailenizin göç hikâyesi' (your family's migration story): followers send a family photo plus a short story, a named jury (the page owner plus a historian or association representative) picks winners against published criteria, and prizes are history books donated by a publisher or association. Publish written rules: dates, criteria, jury, and how winners are announced. Don't make 'tag 3 friends' a requirement (see P3). Get a lawyer's check before launching it.
findings.verify_note: The exemption has conditions, which the researcher left out. If a publisher or company donates the prizes and the contest promotes its books, that could arguably fall under 'marketing a good', which would end the exemption. The 'jury' must judge on stated skill or knowledge criteria. A lawyer check is still needed.
findings.corrected_claim: Under Art. 2(1)(ç) of the 2006 regulation, a skill- or jury-judged 'yarışma' is outside its scope only if two conditions hold. Participants must not be charged anything, and the contest must not be aimed at marketing or selling a good or service. Art. 4(m) defines a yarışma as winners chosen on knowledge, skill or talent, by elimination ranking or by a jury using those criteria; it also covers bilmece, bulmaca and entertainment programs. Art. 2(1)(c) separately exempts set-ups where everyone who meets the announced conditions wins, with no draw at all. Art. 2(1)(f) exempts prizes worth less than 2% of the Law 7338 Art. 4(e) amount (141.2 TL in 2020 per Hukuki Haber; the 2026 figure is not verified).

findings.claim: Mass follow-for-follow, engagement pods and 'tag friends' bait break Meta's rules or get demoted. Following the competitor's roughly 8,000 followers one by one is risky and brings in low-value followers.
findings.detail: Instagram's Community Guidelines ban artificially inflating likes, followers or shares, and repeatedly contacting people for commercial purposes without consent. Its Recommendations Guidelines make accounts that use 'misleading tactics like buying likes' ineligible for recommendation, and treat 'coordinated comment networks meant to artificially boost engagement' as low-quality content. Facebook's ranking explicitly demotes 'Engagement Bait' and clickbait. I found no official Instagram daily follow limit (search budget ran out), so any '150-200 follows/day' figures online are unverified. My own reasoning: many follow-back followers unfollow later or never engage. Since Instagram judges posts by how followers react to them, a large unengaged follower base can lower reach per post.
findings.recommendation: Don't mass-follow the 8,000. If the user does any manual outreach, keep it small, human-paced and personal: reply thoughtfully to people who comment on Rumeli/muhacir posts and follow only genuinely relevant accounts. Never buy followers or likes, never use follow/unfollow bots, and never give the password to any 'growth' app. Put the effort into collaborations (P7) and content good enough to be recommended instead.
findings.verify_note: The Instagram Community Guidelines text is confirmed: 'not artificially collecting likes, followers, or shares, posting repetitive comments or content' and 'repeatedly contacting people for commercial purposes without their consent'. The Recommendations Guidelines confirm that accounts which 'Repeatedly engaged in misleading practices to build followings, such as purchasing likes' are not recommended, and that 'coordinated comment networks intended to artificially drive engagement and distribution' count as low quality. One caveat: Meta's 'Types of content we demote' page (updated 2 Jul 2025) lists Engagement Bait and Clickbait Links, but it covers only Facebook and does not mention Instagram. An official daily follow limit stays not found; I could not search for it either, because the web-search budget was used up. The claim that mass-following the 8,000 is risky rests on reasoning, not on a published rule.

findings.claim: Instagram and Facebook cut recommendations for accounts that mostly repost others' content. Since April 2026 this covers Instagram photos and carousels, not only Reels, which is a direct risk for a history page built on archival images.
findings.detail: Tubefilter, 30 Apr 2026: Instagram extended its unoriginal-content policy to photo and carousel posts. Accounts that repost too many photos or carousels become ineligible for recommendations in feeds and Explore unless the material is significantly changed. What counts as changed: unique text, commentary, voiceover, creative edits. Changing speed or adding a screenshot of the original poster's name does not. Facebook (creators blog, 14 Jul 2025): repeated reuse of others' content means reduced distribution; avoid visible third-party watermarks; adding your own watermark is not a meaningful enhancement; you may share your own content across your own Pages. Instagram has made Reels with other apps' logos or watermarks (e.g., TikTok) 'less discoverable in places like the Reels tab' since 10 Feb 2021.
findings.recommendation: Every post must carry original work: research-based captions with sources, a map or timeline overlay, a 'then and now' comparison, the page's own design template, voiceover narration in Reels. Never repost another page's image or video, especially with their watermark, including Shadows of Rumelia's colorized versions. Export clean, watermark-free files separately for Instagram, TikTok, YouTube Shorts and Facebook. Don't re-upload a video downloaded from TikTok.
findings.verify_note: Tubefilter (30 Apr 2026) confirmed: the policy is extended to photos and carousels. Accounts that repost too much lose eligibility for feed and Discover recommendations unless the material is significantly changed. 'Unique text, creative edits, and voiceover' count as changes; changing speed or adding a screenshot of the original poster's name does not. Followers still see the reposts. The Facebook creators blog (14 Jul 2025) confirmed: reduced distribution and loss of monetization, 'Avoid visible third party watermarks', 'simply stitching together clips or adding your watermark does not qualify', and you may share your own content across your own Pages. Tubefilter (10 Feb 2021) confirmed that Reels carrying the TikTok logo became 'less discoverable in places like the Reels tab'. The Instagram Recommendations Guidelines also say content 'largely repurposed from another source with only minor, immaterial edits' may not be recommended.

findings.claim: Platform reach in Turkey (late 2025 ad-reach data): Instagram 62.3M, YouTube 57.9M, TikTok 44.9M adults, Facebook 34.7M, X 18.5M. WhatsApp isn't covered. Facebook still reaches about half of adults, which matters for older muhacir family members.
findings.detail: DataReportal 'Digital 2026 Turkey' (published 8 Nov 2025, data mostly October 2025): Instagram 70.9% of the population, YouTube 66.0%, TikTok 68.6% of adults, Facebook 39.5% (53.2% of adults; ad audience 64.4% male, 34.2% female), X 21.1%, LinkedIn 23.9%, Snapchat 18.5%, Messenger 14.5%. DataReportal 'Digital 2025 Turkey' (3 Mar 2025) ranks platforms by share of internet users: Instagram 75.6%, YouTube 74.4%, TikTok 52.0%, Facebook 45.0%, X 25.5%. These are ad-reach figures, not active users. I found no age breakdown, so the claim that older muhacir descendants lean toward Facebook and WhatsApp is my own reasoning.
findings.recommendation: Instagram is the main platform. Cut every Reel once and publish it natively to YouTube Shorts, TikTok and Facebook Reels, linking Facebook through Accounts Center. Open a Facebook Page and post natively, with text and photo rather than just a link, to reach parents and grandparents. Open a WhatsApp Channel so older relatives can forward posts into family groups. Design every image to stand on its own, with the logo and handle visible, so forwarded copies lead people back to the page.
findings.verify_note: DataReportal 'Digital 2026 Turkey' (8 Nov 2025) confirmed all figures. Ad reach: Instagram 62.3M (70.9% of the population, 92.1% of adults), YouTube 57.9M (66.0%), TikTok 44.9M aged 18+ (68.6% of adults), Facebook 34.7M (39.5%, 53.2% of adults; 64.4% male / 34.2% female), X 18.5M (21.1%), LinkedIn 21.0M members (23.9%), Snapchat 16.2M (18.5%), Messenger 12.8M (14.5%). 'Digital 2025 Turkey' (3 Mar 2025) confirmed ad reach as a share of internet users: Instagram 75.6%, YouTube 74.4%, TikTok 52.0%, Facebook 45.0%, X 25.5%. These are ad-reach figures, not active users. There are no WhatsApp figures. The age-related reasoning remains the researcher's inference.

findings.claim: Turkish authorities have blocked Instagram outright before, so a page that lives only on Instagram has a real single-platform risk.
findings.detail: CNBC-e, 2 Aug 2024: Instagram was blocked ex officio by BTK decision, with 57 million Turkish users cited. The article does not give the duration. From my own knowledge (not checked this session) it was lifted after about 9 days, on 10 Aug 2024, and there have been later bandwidth-throttling episodes during unrest.
findings.recommendation: From day one, claim the same or a similar handle on TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, X, Threads and a WhatsApp Channel. Back up all source files and captions offline. Keep at least one channel that doesn't depend on Instagram (WhatsApp Channel or YouTube) so the audience isn't lost during a block or an account suspension.
findings.verify_note: CNBC-e (2 Aug 2024) confirmed the ex officio BTK block and the figure of about 57M users. The researcher's unchecked recollection of the duration is now confirmed. English Wikipedia ('Censorship of Instagram') says the block ran from 2 Aug to 10 Aug 2024, called it nine days, and says it was lifted after Instagram agreed to work with the authorities. Turkish Wikipedia says it was imposed under Law 5651 and lifted at 21:30 on 10 Aug 2024 after Minister Uraloğlu's announcement. That is about 8 days, or 9 counting both endpoints. The 'later bandwidth-throttling episodes' (for example March 2025) were NOT verified; neither Wikipedia page I read mentions them.

findings.claim: Collaborations with muhacir associations, academics and Balkan-history YouTubers are the safest fast organic accelerator. BAL-GÖÇ is a verified, social-media-active partner.
findings.detail: BAL-GÖÇ (Balkan Göçmenleri Kültür ve Dayanışma Derneği; balgoc.org.tr) lists 10 branches, all in Bursa districts: Bandırma, Görükle, İnegöl, İznik, Karacabey, Kestel, Mustafakemalpaşa, Orhangazi, Osmangazi and Yenişehir. It runs a folk-dance group, a Rumeli folk music section, a digital library of theses and biographies, children's courses and scholarships, and has Facebook, X, Instagram, LinkedIn, YouTube and WhatsApp accounts. Contact is through the site's İletişim (contact) page, phone +90 224 240 1111, WhatsApp +90 501 304 1400. Lozan Mübadilleri Vakfı's site returned 503, so I couldn't verify it. I couldn't verify other federations (Western Thrace, Bulgarian, Kosovo associations) or Shadows of Rumelia's details because the search budget ran out. Details of how Instagram Collab posts work (one post on both grids, shared to both audiences, a few co-authors allowed) come from my own knowledge, not a source fetched this session.
findings.recommendation: Pitch partners with a finished piece of work, not a request for a shoutout. For example: 'We prepared a carousel on the Rumeli muhacir villages of İnegöl. May we publish it as a joint Collab post with your logo?' Offer associations and their members free digitization and storytelling of family photos and documents, credited to the family. For academics, turn a published article into a carousel with a full citation and invite them as co-author. For YouTubers and podcasters, offer a guest Q&A or a joint Reel. Approach the competitor for a friendly collaboration rather than poaching its followers. Aim for 1-2 Collabs per week in the first month.
sources: no source for Collab feature mechanics; my own reasoning (search budget exhausted)
findings.verify_note: The site itself does not state which province each branch is in; 'all in Bursa districts' was the researcher's inference, and it is wrong for Bandırma. I could not verify the Collab mechanics either, since the Instagram help page did not load and the search budget was gone. The rest of P7 is a strategy recommendation and needs no fact-check.
findings.corrected_claim: BAL-GÖÇ (Balkan Göçmenleri Kültür ve Dayanışma Derneği) lists 10 branches: Bandırma, Görükle, İnegöl, İznik, Karacabey, Kestel, Mustafakemalpaşa, Orhangazi, Osmangazi and Yenişehir. Most are in Bursa, but Bandırma is a district of Balıkesir province, and Görükle is a neighbourhood of Nilüfer (Bursa), not a district. Its social accounts are Instagram @balgocgenelmerkez, X @bursabalgoc, Facebook BalgocGenelMerkez, YouTube @balgocgenelmerkez8980 and a LinkedIn page. Phone +90 224 240 1111, WhatsApp +90 501 304 14 00.

findings.claim: Meta ads in Turkey are cheap by global standards, but the only 2026 Turkey CPM figures are unmethodical web compilations, and I found no reliable cost-per-follower or cost-per-profile-visit figure.
findings.detail: Stackmatix (6 Sep 2026, no methodology or data source stated): Turkey CPM $2.00-4.40, up 9% year on year. Adligator (undated): Turkey $2.00-3.50 and $3.00-5.00 in two unlabeled columns. Braverytechnology (Turkish agency page, labeled 2026 data): Instagram CPM 15-120 TL, CPC 1.5-50 TL. Webtekno says around 20 TL a day is commonly suggested as the minimum budget in Turkey. Not found: any credible TL cost per follower or profile visit for Turkey in 2025-2026. Searched in Turkish and English for CPM, takipçi başı (cost per follower) and profile visits.
findings.recommendation: Don't pay to boost the launch post. Wait 1-2 weeks, then put a small test budget (for example 100-200 TL a day for 5-7 days) behind the best-performing organic Reel. Use the Instagram profile-visit objective in Ads Manager rather than 'engagement', and Reels/Feed placements only, with Audience Network off. Measure the real cost per follower as spend divided by net new follows minus unfollows a week later. Scale only if those followers engage.
findings.verify_note: Stackmatix (6 Sep 2026) confirmed: Turkey CPM $2.00-4.40, +9% year on year, no methodology or data source. Braverytechnology confirmed: a '2026 Aralığı' of CPM 15-120 TL and CPC 1.5-50 TL, based on 'müşteri kampanyaları ve sektörel raporlar' (its own client campaigns and sector reports), with no sample size given. I did not re-check Adligator or the Webtekno 20 TL/day figure. The researcher's own low-confidence framing is accurate.

findings.claim: Meta now adds a 5% 'location fee' to ads shown in Turkey, invoiced separately on top of the budget, and VAT can come on top of that. Budget for roughly 1.25x the stated ad spend.
findings.detail: Social Media Today (10 Mar 2026): Meta passes location-specific costs such as digital service taxes on to advertisers in Austria, France, Italy, Spain, Türkiye (5%) and the UK. Start dates conflict: ShiftDelete (12 Mar 2026) says 1 Oct 2026, Webtekno (24 Jun 2026) says 1 Jul 2026. Either way the fee is in effect by November 2026. It depends on where the ads are shown, not where the advertiser is based, and appears as its own invoice line (Webtekno example: 5 TL on a 100 TL ad). Turkish accounting sites say foreign ad services are subject to KDV (VAT), with 20% as the general rate in 2026; one site says 18%, and Log says KDV is added on top. My rough estimate is 1,000 TL x 1.05 x 1.20 = about 1,260 TL; check it against the actual Meta invoice. Card payment problems (online or foreign-transaction permissions on Turkish cards) are my own reasoning and weren't checked.
findings.recommendation: Calculate ad budgets including the 5% location fee and VAT. Use a card with online and international transactions enabled, set the ad account currency to TL, and keep the invoices. If the page later becomes a business, ask a mali müşavir (accountant) about VAT and withholding.
findings.verify_note: Two corrections. (1) The start date conflict is settled in favour of 1 July 2026 by the quoted Meta email; either way the fee is in effect by November 2026. (2) The researcher wrote that 'Log says KDV is added on top'. The Log article does NOT mention KDV at all. The 20% rate comes from eleman.net, and that page covers only businesses, not individuals. The ~1.26x estimate is still a reasonable rough budget figure, but it is unsourced.
findings.corrected_claim: Meta charges a 5% location fee on ads delivered to audiences in Türkiye. Other rates: Austria 5%, France, Italy and Spain 3%, UK 2%. It is based on where the ad is delivered and billed as its own line, separate from the budget. According to the Meta advertiser email quoted by Log (23 Jun 2026) and Webtekno (24 Jun 2026), it took effect on 1 July 2026. ShiftDelete's '1 Oct 2026' looks wrong. VAT: eleman.net (18 Apr 2025) says businesses must account for 20% KDV on foreign ad services as imported services, declared on the '2 No.lu KDV beyannamesi' (VAT return no. 2).

findings.claim: Paid targeting can reach the Rumeli and Balkan Turkish audience only through geography, language and interests, not ethnic origin. Turkish-speaking areas of the Balkans can be targeted alongside Turkish cities.
findings.detail: From my own knowledge (not checked this session): Meta removed detailed-targeting options touching sensitive topics such as ethnicity and political beliefs in 2022. City or radius targeting (Edirne, Kırklareli, Tekirdağ, Bursa, İzmir, Manisa, Eskişehir, İstanbul) and interest targeting (Ottoman Empire, Balkans, history) remain available, and ads can also be aimed at Turkish speakers in Bulgaria (e.g., Kardzhali/Kırcaali, Shumen/Şumnu), Greece (Komotini/Gümülcine, Xanthi/İskeçe), North Macedonia and Kosovo. Ads touching current social or political issues may fall under Meta's special ad category for social issues, elections or politics, which needs authorization; I couldn't verify how this applies in Turkey.
findings.recommendation: Build two test ad sets: (a) Turkey, the Marmara/Aegean cities above, ages 25-65, Turkish language, history/Ottoman/Balkan interests; (b) Turkish-language users in Bulgaria, Greece (Thrace), North Macedonia and Kosovo. Keep ad creative purely historical and cultural so it isn't classed as political.
sources: no source; my own reasoning (search budget exhausted, Meta ads policy pages not fetched)
findings.verify_note: Only one part is verified. Meta announced on 9 Nov 2021 that it would remove Detailed Targeting options tied to health, race and ethnicity, political affiliation, religion and sexual orientation, effective 19 Jan 2022. 'Removed in 2022' is therefore roughly right: announced in 2021, effective in 2022. I did not verify the rest. That includes current interest options such as Ottoman Empire or Balkans, Turkish-language targeting in Bulgaria, Greece, North Macedonia and Kosovo, and whether Meta's social-issues ad authorization applies in Turkey. I could not search, because the budget was exhausted.

findings.claim: Balkan history topics draw nationalist comment raids and mass-reporting. Wording that attacks nations instead of describing documented events risks removal under the hate-speech rules and makes the page an easier target.
findings.detail: Instagram's Community Guidelines ban attacks on people based on protected characteristics, but allow hateful material shared to challenge it or raise awareness when that intent is clearly stated. Reports go to a global review team plus automated systems. Meta's pages I checked don't say whether the number of reports affects removal; I found nothing on that. Details of mass-reporting campaigns by Greek, Bulgarian, Serbian, Albanian, Macedonian or Bosniak nationalist users are not documented in what I could check (search budget exhausted). The sensitivities are my own reasoning: 1912-13 atrocities, the 1989 Bulgarian expulsion, Bosniak/Albanian versus Turkish identity claims, and 'lost lands' rhetoric.
findings.recommendation: Avoid irredentist framing such as 'kayıp topraklarımız' (our lost lands), 'geri alacağız' (we will take it back), 'X milleti hain/düşman' (nation X are traitors/enemies), or 'Yunan/Bulgar/Sırp vahşeti' (Greek/Bulgarian/Serbian savagery) applied to a whole people. Prefer 'belgelenmiş olaylar' (documented events), name the specific units, bands or governments responsible with dates and sources, and give both the Turkish and current names of places, e.g. 'Selanik (Thessaloniki)'. Before launch, set Hidden Words (custom slur list in Turkish, Greek, Bulgarian, Serbian and Albanian) and turn on Limit Interactions during raids. Don't fight in the comments. Report organized abuse, and keep screenshots for appeals.
findings.verify_note: The Community Guidelines confirm the exception: 'When hateful conduct is being shared to challenge it or to raise awareness, we may allow it.' Meta's January 2025 announcement also says it removed some restrictions on politically debated topics such as immigration and gender. That shows hateful-conduct enforcement changed during 2025, but I found nothing specific to Balkan topics. Mass-reporting campaigns and whether report counts affect removals remain not found; I could not search. The specific sensitivities are reasoning, not sourced fact.

findings.claim: Graphic atrocity or war photos are allowed when shared to educate, with a warning, but Instagram won't recommend graphic violence. Massacre-heavy posts will get little non-follower reach.
findings.detail: Instagram's Community Guidelines allow newsworthy graphic content shared to condemn, raise awareness or educate, suggest adding a warning, and say images shared 'for sadistic pleasure or to glorify violence' are never allowed. Its Recommendations Guidelines list 'graphic or disturbing violence' among content not recommended. They also make ineligible accounts that recently broke the guidelines or repeatedly use sensitive content in their name, username, photo or bio.
findings.recommendation: For the Balkan Wars, the 1912-13 expulsions and the like, tell the story through maps, refugee columns, documents, survivor testimonies and portraits instead of corpses. If a graphic image is historically essential, put it on a later slide (never the cover), add a 'hassas içerik' (sensitive content) warning, and frame it as remembrance, not revenge.
findings.verify_note: The substance holds. The exact phrase 'graphic or disturbing violence' was not found verbatim in the Recommendations Guidelines. 'Sensitive content in name/bio' is better described as content Instagram tries not to recommend appearing in the name, username, profile photo or bio.
findings.corrected_claim: Community Guidelines: users who share violent news content to condemn it or raise awareness are encouraged to add a warning, and 'Sharing graphic images for sadistic pleasure or to glorify violence is never allowed.' Recommendations Guidelines: 'Content that may depict violence, such as people fighting' may not be recommended, and most graphic and disturbing imagery is hidden from teens even where adults would see it behind a warning screen. Accounts that 'repeatedly and/or recently shared content we try not to recommend in the account name, username, profile photo, bio' are not recommended.

findings.claim: Most pre-1912 photos are in the public domain under Turkish law if the photographer died more than 70 years ago. Modern scans, colorizations and other pages' edits can still bring IP complaints, and Instagram removes content on valid reports.
findings.detail: FSEK (Law 5846) Art. 27, as summarized on Wikimedia Commons: protection lasts for the author's life plus 70 years; anonymous works and works of legal persons are protected for 70 years from publication. The separate photo rule (Art. 29) was repealed on 12 Feb 2001, so photos follow the general rule. Freedom of panorama (Art. 40) covers only exterior architecture and permanently placed art. Instagram's Community Guidelines say to share 'only photos and videos that you've taken or have the right to share' and let rights holders file copyright reports. The Library of Congress Abdul Hamid II collection page returned 403, so I couldn't verify its rights statement this session. My own reasoning on music: commercial songs on cross-posted YouTube Shorts and TikTok can trigger copyright claims, and Instagram's in-app library is narrower for Business accounts than for Creator accounts (not verified this session).
findings.recommendation: Get images from sources with clear public-domain status (Wikimedia Commons items tagged PD-Turkey or PD-old, institutions' open-access collections) and credit the source and catalog number on every post. Don't use other pages' colorized or AI-restored versions, or stock-agency watermarked images. For music, use the in-app library or royalty-free tracks, and consider a Creator account for the wider music catalog.
findings.verify_note: Wikimedia Commons (Turkey) confirms: life plus 70 years (Art. 27); anonymous and legal-person works run 70 years from when the work was made public; the photo and film rule in Art. 29 was repealed on 12 Feb 2001, so photos follow the general term; before 1995 the term was 50 years. Freedom of panorama (Art. 40) covers only fine-art works permanently placed on public streets, avenues or squares, and only the exterior of architecture. The guidelines line 'Share only photos and videos that you've taken or have the right to share' is confirmed. The music-library claims, and the Library of Congress rights statement, were not verified.

findings.claim: Fake 'copyright violation' and 'verification badge' DMs are the most common way new pages get hijacked. Instagram says it never DMs users about copyright.
findings.detail: BGR (29 Mar 2021) quotes Instagram: 'Instagram will never DM you about Copyright violations... DO NOT CLICK OR REPLY.' Real messages appear under Settings > Security > Emails from Instagram: 'Nothing there? Then it's not from us.' Kaspersky documented phishing pages that copy Instagram's copyright appeal form. Gridinsoft (2026 roundup) and isthisascam list fake blue-badge or Meta Verified offers and 'your account will be deleted in 24 hours' lures. One roundup cites Meta taking down 10.9M accounts linked to scam centers in 2025; I didn't verify that figure directly.
findings.recommendation: Before launch: turn on two-factor authentication with an authenticator app rather than SMS, store the backup codes offline, use a unique password and a dedicated email, and link the account in Accounts Center. Never log in through a link sent by DM or email. Check notices only under Emails from Instagram and Account Status. Never pay for a 'blue tick' through a DM, and never share the password with growth services or so-called collab managers.
findings.verify_note: BGR (29 Mar 2021) quotes Instagram: 'Instagram will never DM you about Copyright violations or ever ask for any of your personal details like passwords etc.' It names Settings > Security > Emails From Instagram as the place to check. Kaspersky's post is dated 15 Mar 2019 and describes phishing by EMAIL ('permanently deleted for copyright infringement', with a fake appeal page that asks for the login and then the email password), not by DM. Gridinsoft was last updated 13 Sep 2026; it lists copyright-warning and blue-badge lures. It cites the 10.9M scam-center accounts taken down in 2025 to a Meta post of 11 Mar 2026, 'Fighting Scammers and Protecting People With New Technology and Partnerships', which I did not open directly. 'Most common way' is not quantified by any source.

findings.claim: Getting history wrong is both a reach risk and a reputation risk. Content rated false or altered and photorealistic AI images without a label can make the account ineligible for recommendation, and Turkish fact-checkers actively debunk viral history claims.
findings.detail: Instagram's Recommendations Guidelines: in countries with third-party fact-checking, content rated false isn't recommended. Accounts that recently and repeatedly posted content rated 'False' or 'Altered', or that repeatedly share photorealistic AI-generated people without an AI label, become ineligible for recommendation. Doğruluk Payı runs a 'Tarih ve Dezenformasyon' series and has checked claims such as an Atatürk white-horse photo, an alleged Atatürk letter to the Saudi king, Ottoman literacy rates and Abdülhamid II claims; it also takes reader tips. Teyit.org returned 403, so its current scope and Meta-partner status weren't verified this session. Common pitfalls (my own reasoning): made-up 'Fatih/Atatürk said' quotes, Balkan photos mislabeled as Anatolia or the reverse, and AI 'old photos' passed off as real.
findings.recommendation: Cite a source on every post (archive and catalog number, book and page). Never post a quote you can't trace to a primary or scholarly source. Label colorized or AI-restored images, e.g. 'yapay zekâ ile renklendirilmiştir' (colorized with AI), and never post AI-generated scenes as real photos. Run a reverse image search before posting. Pin a short corrections note ('Hata görürseniz bildirin', i.e. tell us if you spot an error) and publicly correct mistakes; that builds trust with the academics and associations the page wants as partners.
findings.verify_note: The Recommendations Guidelines confirm: in countries with third-party fact-checking, accounts that recently and repeatedly posted content rated False or Altered are not recommended, and neither are accounts that repeatedly share content featuring a photorealistic AI-generated person without the AI label. Meta's fact-checking page says the program is ending in the US but still relies on certified fact-checkers elsewhere, and still 'dramatically reduce[s] the distribution of False and Altered posts'. Minor correction: on Doğruluk Payı, 'Tarih ve Dezenformasyon' is Episode 1 of a 'Tarih Mitleri' series under Originals, not a standalone series. The examples are confirmed: the Atatürk white-horse photo, the letter to the Saudi king, the 66% Ottoman literacy table, and Abdülhamid and the kara çarşaf. A 'Şüpheli İddia İlet' (submit a suspicious claim) form exists. Doğruluk Payı's About page lists 'META – Ticari Anlaşma' (a commercial agreement with Meta) among its 2025 revenues and says it was a founding IFCN advisory board member. That suggests an active Meta relationship, but it does not confirm a fact-checking partnership in Turkey. teyit.org still returns 403.

findings.claim: Facebook groups, Reddit and Ekşi Sözlük can reach large niche audiences, but each has anti-promotion norms. Dropping links tends to get removed or backfire.
findings.detail: My own reasoning, unverified: Ekşi's rules page returned 403 and the search budget ran out before I could check Reddit or Facebook-group rules. Many hometown, village and muhacir Facebook groups ban promotion without admin approval. Reddit communities (r/Turkey, history subreddits) usually enforce self-promotion limits. Ekşi Sözlük users and moderators react badly to 'reklam' (advertising) entries.
findings.recommendation: In Facebook groups, ask admins first, then post the full content natively (image and text) with a small credit instead of a bare link, and answer comments personally. On Reddit and Ekşi, contribute sourced information as a person; mention the page only where it's relevant and allowed. Treat these as secondary channels after Instagram, Collabs, Facebook, YouTube and TikTok.
sources: no source; my own reasoning (eksisozluk.com/kurallar returned 403; search budget exhausted)
findings.verify_note: This is the researcher's own reasoning with no sources. My web-search budget was exhausted on my first query, so I could not check Ekşi, Reddit or Facebook-group rules. It is plausible but unverified.

findings.claim: Paid boosts can bring low-quality or off-target engagement, and I found no authoritative data on whether boosted followers stay or engage.
findings.detail: Search results were mostly vendor blogs. One Reddit anecdote describes boost engagement from accounts far outside the target audience, and vendor blogs claim profile-destination ads beat boosted posts on cost per follower. None of this is independent evidence. Not found: Meta documentation or independent studies on how good boosted followers are.
findings.recommendation: Treat paid reach as an amplifier for posts that are already proven, not as a growth engine. Check the quality of new followers: real profiles, Turkish or Balkan location, whether they interact. Stop any ad set that brings follows without saves or shares.
findings.verify_note: The sources are vendor blogs, which I did not re-check, plus one Reddit anecdote. There is no independent data, and I could not search. The researcher's own low-confidence label stands.

refuted.claim: Instagram and Threads don't proactively recommend 'political content' (laws, elections, social topics) by default. Rumeli posts that drift into current politics can lose Explore and Reels reach, and professional accounts can see this in Account Status.
refuted.detail: Instagram announcement of 9 Feb 2024 (updated 7 Jan 2025 and 28 May 2025): political content is not proactively recommended on Explore, Reels, in-feed recommendations or Suggested Users unless the viewer opts in, but followers still see it. Professional accounts can check their recommendation eligibility in Account Status, then edit or delete posts, request a review, or pause that kind of posting to become eligible again. Posts about current minority rights in Western Thrace or Bulgaria, Kosovo politics, Turkish foreign-policy debates or election-period topics plausibly fall under 'social topics'. That classification is my own reasoning.
refuted.recommendation: Keep at least 80-90% of posts strictly historical, cultural, culinary, folkloric or family-memory content. When covering a current issue, do it rarely and in neutral language. Use a Professional (Creator or Business) account and check Account Status weekly, especially after any spike in reports.
refuted.verify_note: The Instagram blog post the researcher relied on is from 9 Feb 2024. Its 7 Jan 2025 and 28 May 2025 updates only point readers to the newsroom and the Transparency Center, and those pages describe the reversal. Account Status still exists for professional accounts. Advising mostly historical, cultural content is still sensible for other reasons: comment raids, reports, and the page's credibility. But the specific reach mechanism the researcher described is out of date.
refuted.corrected_claim: Meta's current policy (Transparency Center, updated 18 Sep 2025) treats political content 'more like other types of content'. It ranks it with personalized signals and 'may recommend political content from accounts people don't already follow' on Facebook, Instagram and Threads. Users can raise or lower how much they see. This follows Meta's 7 Jan 2025 'More Speech and Fewer Mistakes' announcement, which phased civic content back in with a personalized approach. Political content is therefore no longer simply excluded from recommendations by default.

missed_points: Method note: the shared WebSearch budget ran out on my first query. Every check above was done with direct WebFetch of the cited or known primary URLs. Points marked unverifiable might be checkable with a fresh search budget.

Meta's political-content policy reversed during 2025. Since 18 Sep 2025 the Transparency Center says political content is ranked like other content and may be recommended from accounts people don't follow, with user controls (https://transparency.meta.com/features/approach-to-political-content/, after https://about.fb.com/news/2025/01/meta-more-speech-fewer-mistakes/ of 7 Jan 2025). Any advice built on 'political posts get zero Explore reach' is outdated. The more relevant risks for Rumeli content are reports and hateful-conduct enforcement.

The legal alternative to a draw is narrower than the researcher said, and there is a second exemption they missed. Under Art. 2(1)(c) of the 2006 MPİ regulation, set-ups where EVERYONE who meets the announced conditions wins, with no draw, are excluded. Example: every follower who sends a family migration story gets featured or receives a digital certificate. The yarışma exemption in Art. 2(1)(ç) applies only if entry is free and the contest is not aimed at marketing or selling a good or service. Book prizes from a sponsoring publisher could undercut that (https://www.resmigazete.gov.tr/eskiler/2006/10/20061004-10.htm).

Art. 10(2) of the regulation adds heavy operational duties for any permitted online draw: collect each entrant's name, address and a code, notify winners by registered mail, and submit electronic participant records to MPİ before the draw. That makes an 'Instagram comment giveaway' impractical even with a permit (https://www.resmigazete.gov.tr/eskiler/2006/10/20061004-10.htm).

The penalty framing for unauthorized giveaways is inconsistent across sources. Gazete Vatan (12 Jan 2021) reported up to 2 years in prison and an administrative fine of up to 10M TL; Şimşek (26 Jan 2025) said 3-6 years plus a judicial fine. Hukuki Haber cites only TCK 157 (fraud, for undelivered prizes). The current statutory basis is unidentified, so the user should not rely on any single penalty number (https://www.gazetevatan.com/magazin/korsan-cekilis-yapan-fenomenlere-para-cezasi-10-milyon-lira-1366457, https://www.ekonomist.com.tr/haberler/simsek-ten-izinsiz-cekilis-uyarisi-hapis-cezasi-var-56988).

MPİ's homepage links a 'Çekiliş İzinleri' (draw permits) section and an online permit platform, cekilisevi.gov.tr, which returned 503 when I tried it. The homepage also says under-18s may not take part in the eşya piyangoları that MPİ itself runs. Any history-page contest that might attract teenagers should check the age rules (https://www.mpi.gov.tr/).

Meta's 'Types of content we demote' page (updated 2 Jul 2025) covers only Facebook. Separately, in January 2025 Meta said it was 'getting rid of most of these demotions' and requiring greater confidence for the rest. Demotion-based warnings should be framed as Instagram Recommendations Guidelines eligibility rules, which are confirmed, rather than as Facebook feed demotions (https://transparency.meta.com/features/approach-to-ranking/types-of-content-we-demote/, https://about.fb.com/news/2025/01/meta-more-speech-fewer-mistakes/).

Instagram hides most graphic and disturbing imagery from teen accounts even when adults would see it behind a warning screen. Atrocity-heavy Balkan Wars posts will reach even less of a young audience (https://www.facebook.com/help/instagram/313829416281232).

Shadows of Rumelia's handle, follower count (~8,000) and content were NOT verified. Fetching instagram.com/shadowsofrumelia (a guessed handle) returned HTTP 429, and I could not search. Treat the 8,000 figure as the user's own estimate.

Not verified (no search budget): Instagram hashtag-count limits introduced in 2025-2026, the current Collab co-author limit, Trial Reels availability, and any official daily follow/action limit. The researcher should not state these as fact without a fresh check.
